false_positives.candidate:
Export (and Pause) abilities restricted to alerting rules, recording rules lose Export in list view

In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, ModifyExport is computed as [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed] where isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The ruler-based equivalent uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule = rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule), which matches both Grafana alerting AND recording rules, so recording rules currently expose the 'Export / With modifications' menu item (the modify-export flow supports recording rules). In the new ruler-less list view the rulerRule is absent, so canExport relies solely on the prom-based ability and recording rules lose the Export menu entry. The same narrowing applies to Pause/Restore (Grafana recording rules are pausable, but the prom-based ability requires an alerting rule), which will bite once the pause menu item is wired to prom rules.

Federated rule groups lose their immutable treatment after useAllAlertRuleAbilities refactor

Before this change, useAllAlertRuleAbilities (still used via useAlertRuleAbility by CombinedRule consumers such as the existing RulesTable) computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made Update/Delete/Pause unsupported for federated (cross-tenant) Mimir/GEM rule groups. The hook now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only receives a RulerRuleDTO and hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. Consequently, for rules in federated groups the Edit/Delete/Pause abilities become 'supported' again and the corresponding buttons/menu items reappear; attempting the operation will fail against the ruler or, worse, modify a group the UI intentionally treated as immutable. The federated check needs to be preserved somewhere in the new delegation chain.

Rule link no longer carries the returnTo parameter

The previous GrafanaRuleListItem (in the deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx) built the rule href as createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo }) using createReturnTo(), so navigating back from the rule detail view returned the user to the originating (possibly filtered) rule list. The new component builds `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` with no returnTo, so the detail view's back navigation falls back to the default alert list and loses the user's list context/filters. Re-add the returnTo parameter.

Stale comment about preloading ruler rules after ruler prefetch was removed

The diff removes the alertRuleApi prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...) dispatch but leaves the comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX. Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded' and the variable name cacheAndRulerPreload. The comment now describes behavior that no longer exists and is misleading about what the remaining upsertQueryData does; update the comment and rename the variable.

skipToken path returns enabled abilities, granting Duplicate on cloud rules based on Grafana permissions

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities/useGrafanaPromRuleAbility translate skipToken into `undefined` and call useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined). With rule undefined, useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns loading:false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported, isPluginProvided/isProvisioned are false, and the abilities are computed with getRulesPermissions('grafana'): Duplicate becomes [true, ctx.hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]. AlertRuleMenu passes skipToken whenever promRule is not a Grafana prom rule (i.e. for every cloud/Mimir rule), and computes canDuplicate as ruler || grafana. As a result a user who has the Grafana-managed rule create permission but NOT AlertingRuleExternalWrite will now see the Duplicate menu item on cloud rules (previously only the ruler-based ability, which checks the external-write permission for that data source, was used). The skipToken/undefined-rule path should yield all-disabled abilities instead of permission-evaluated ones.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting defeats the $__range no-splitting guard

runSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 299) before partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query)) runs on the next line. applyTemplateVariables substitutes the built-in range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from scopedVars, and dashboard/Explore requests always carry those scoped vars. querySupportsSplitting() decides a query must not be split by calling isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr), which searches for the literal text '$__range' — but by the time it runs, that text has already been replaced (e.g. count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) has become count_over_time({a="b"}[30d])). Consequence: queries using $__range are now time-split instead of being routed to nonSplittingQueries and executed once over the full range, which is exactly what the comment above the check says must not happen. Besides contradicting the documented intent, this is a real cost/correctness regression for large ranges: with a 30-day dashboard, each 1-day chunk evaluates count_over_time(...[30d]), re-scanning ~30 days of data per chunk (~30x the scanned volume of the previous single request). The existing unit tests do not catch this because the test requests carry no scopedVars, so $__range survives interpolation in tests but not in production. The isQueryWithRangeVariable check should run on the raw, pre-interpolation expr — or, if splitting such queries is now intentional, the dead check and its misleading comment should be removed.

Queries are now interpolated two to three times (runShardSplitQuery / runSplitQuery / runQuery)

Interpolation is now applied repeatedly to the same targets. LokiDatasource.runQuery — which the splitting code calls for every sub-request (runSplitGroupedQueries in querySplitting.ts, and splitQueriesByStreamShard here) — already maps targets through applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). With the new .map(...) added here in runShardSplitQuery and the one added in runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts), every sub-query in the time-splitting path is interpolated twice, and every sub-query in the shard-splitting path three times (runShardSplitQuery → runSplitQuery → runQuery), because sub-requests keep the original request.scopedVars and request.filters. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters from request.filters are injected into the stream selector on every pass, so the LogQL selectors sent to Loki contain each ad hoc matcher two or three times (previously they were injected exactly once, in runQuery); (2) any variable value that itself contains template syntax (a constant/text variable holding a literal containing another variable's name, or a $-prefixed token) is interpolated again by the later passes, silently altering the query Loki executes. The updated shard-splitting test that expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single-target request (1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 1 per shard group in runSplitQuery, with runQuery mocked) shows the redundancy is being baked into the tests rather than eliminated. One of the interpolation layers should be removed (or the later passes skipped for already-interpolated targets).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID field dropped from "Plugin Request Completed" log lines

Before this change, LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended a "traceID" field to every "Plugin Request Completed" log line via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false). This PR removes that code (and the tracing import) and relies entirely on contextual attributes attached by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware — but instrumentContext in contextual_logger_middleware.go only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it never adds traceID. Nothing else in the plugin client middleware chain attaches traceID via log.WithContextualAttributes, so these log lines lose the trace ID whenever an upstream HTTP middleware hasn't already put it into the context — e.g. plugin calls originating from background services such as alerting evaluations, where the trace exists only as a span in ctx. This breaks log-to-trace correlation that previously always worked. Fix by either keeping the explicit traceID param in LoggerMiddleware or adding traceID inside instrumentContext.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh instance, so logs via FromContext are never recorded

TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(). This matters because the production code changed in this PR (LoggerMiddleware) now logs exclusively through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...). Any test that injects a *TestLogger and then asserts on InfoLogs/ErrorLogs/etc. of the instance it holds will see zero recorded calls — tests expecting a log will fail confusingly, and tests asserting that nothing was logged will silently false-pass even though the code under test did log. The fake should return f (or record into shared state) so that logs written through FromContext are observable by the test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running earlier in the chain

LoggerMiddleware previously built the pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, and dsUID log fields itself from req.PluginContext, so it was self-contained. After this change those fields only appear if ContextualLoggerMiddleware ran earlier in the middleware stack and attached them as contextual attributes. The production wiring in CreateMiddlewares happens to order them correctly, but NewLoggerMiddleware is exported and can be composed into other middleware stacks (tests, other decorator constructions); in any stack without ContextualLoggerMiddleware ahead of it, the "Plugin Request Completed" lines lose all plugin-identifying fields with no error or warning. At minimum the ordering requirement should be documented on NewLoggerMiddleware (the old InstrumentationMiddleware had such a comment, and it was removed in the rename).

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test, and no test covers the moved log fields

The PR adds a new middleware (ContextualLoggerMiddleware) responsible for attaching endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname to the request context, but adds no test verifying those attributes are attached, and the renamed metrics_middleware_test.go only covers the prometheus metrics. There is also no test asserting that LoggerMiddleware's "Plugin Request Completed" output still contains the fields that were moved out of it — which is exactly why the traceID regression introduced by this PR (the explicit traceID field was removed and is no longer added anywhere in the chain) is not caught by the test suite. A small test chaining ContextualLoggerMiddleware + LoggerMiddleware and asserting the resulting log fields would lock in the intended behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-act race between CountDevices and the insert allows exceeding the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first calling CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT/upsert. The count and the insert are separate, non-transactional queries. Two concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the anon_device table ends up with more devices than the configured limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (e.g., a public dashboard link being opened by many clients at once, or multiple Grafana HA replicas), the limit is only a soft cap. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a single statement with a subquery guard, a transaction with appropriate isolation, or an INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed on retry because the local cache is populated before the store write succeeds

In tagDeviceUI, the device cache key is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) at line 87) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first request from a new device is correctly rejected in the anonymous auth client (client.go returns the error). However, the cache entry remains for ~29 minutes (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)). Any subsequent request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the store, and the anonymous authentication succeeds. The consequence is that the new configurable device limit is effectively unenforced: a blocked device only sees one failed request and then gets full anonymous access by simply retrying (e.g., refreshing the browser), with the block re-asserting only once per 29-minute cache-expiry window. The cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (or the key must be removed when it returns an error).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved from background goroutine into the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and a recover() guard, so anonymous authentication never blocked on the database write and a panic in tagging could not affect the request. This PR calls TagDevice synchronously in Authenticate for all deployments, including the default case where device_limit is unset (0) and the enforcement is not needed. On every local-cache miss (roughly once per 29 minutes per device) each anonymous request now waits for the COUNT + upsert round trips before an identity is returned, and a panic in the tagging path now propagates into request handling. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when the limit is disabled, or restoring the timeout/recover protection.

New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini

The PR introduces cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from key 'device_limit' in the [auth.anonymous] section, but it does not add the option to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where the other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented with comments. As shipped, the setting is undiscoverable for administrators and its semantics (0 = unlimited, limit counted over devices active in the last 30 days) are undocumented.

No test for the allowed path (existing device updated when limit is reached) or for repeated rejection

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a brand-new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is hit. Two important behaviors are untested: (1) that a device already present in anon_device is still successfully updated (updateDevice returns nil) when count >= deviceLimit — this is the intended happy path that keeps existing devices working, and a regression there would lock out legitimate users; (2) that a rejected device keeps being rejected on subsequent TagDevice/CreateOrUpdateDevice attempts — a test through AnonDeviceService.TagDevice would have caught the local-cache bypass where the second request from a blocked device succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level on every cycle

The new cleanup code logs normal, healthy operation with r.log.Error at six sites: lines 534, 537 ("Annotations to clean by time" / "cleaned annotations by time"), 554, 557 (count variants), and 576, 579 ("Tags to clean" / "cleaned tags"). These fire on every cleanup run even when there is nothing to delete (count=0), include the full ID list (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, e.g. tens of thousands), and carry a nil "err" key. Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to every minute in cleanup.go, this produces a constant stream of ERROR log lines per Grafana instance in the healthy case, which will break error-rate-based alerting/monitoring and inflate log volume. These look like debugging leftovers and should be Debug level (and probably not log raw ID slices).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs

The PR, which is scoped to the annotation cleanup deadlock, changes the CleanUpService ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often on every Grafana instance: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history rows (including the two EnforceRowLimit queries), scanning/removing temp files, plus the annotation cleanup itself. That is a significant, undocumented increase in background DB and disk load, and it also increases how often annotation deletes race with annotation inserts — the exact contention this PR is trying to defuse. If this is intentional it needs justification in the PR and ideally a config option; if it is a leftover from local deadlock reproduction, it should be reverted.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite inline-ID path builds SQL with quadratic string copying

In the SQLite branch of deleteByIDs the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n^2) work. With the batch size this path is designed for (e.g. 32767 IDs, as exercised by the new test), that is on the order of gigabytes of byte copying per batch, repeated on every cleanup cycle while a backlog exists. Using a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-formatted values) would make it linear.

deleteByIDs only guards SQLite's parameter limit; oversized batch sizes fail on Postgres/MySQL

deleteByIDs builds DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with one bind parameter per ID and only switches away from parameters for SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999. On other databases the batch size is configurable and unvalidated: if it is set above the driver's bind-parameter cap (65535 for Postgres, and MySQL prepared statements have a similar 65535 placeholder limit), every cleanup batch will fail with a parameter-count error, so cleanup never makes progress. The previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter list at all, so this is a regression for large configured batch sizes. Consider chunking the ID slice to a safe per-statement size (e.g. 1000) for all dialects.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the bare logger (d.Log) in the context instead of the enriched one

Delete builds a contextual logger with log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then puts the bare logger into the context: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). Downstream log lines emitted from the storage layers lose the name/kind/method identifying fields. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log), consistent with the other methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records the legacy operation result in the storage-duration metric

In DeleteCollection's async goroutine, the outcome of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy), attributing legacy latency and failures to the unified-storage metric. Every other path uses recordLegacyDuration for legacy operations; this should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind as metric label

On successful Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call passes options.Kind as the metric label. Object names (e.g. playlist UIDs) are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus time series — a cardinality explosion — and the metric stops aggregating per kind.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the asynchronous legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is created with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), deriving from the incoming request context. In the Kubernetes API server the request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write completes. The detached goroutine therefore almost always executes with an already-canceled context and the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' — in mode 3 the legacy copy (the stated 'safe measure') is silently skipped, with only a metric recording the failure. The goroutine should first detach values from the request lifecycle, e.g. ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the 10s timeout.

Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy-only objects can never be deleted

Delete now returns immediately on any error from unified storage, including NotFound. The previous implementation special-cased apierrors.IsNotFound and still issued the legacy delete. With the new early return, an object that exists only in legacy storage (created before unified storage was enabled, or left behind by a failed dual write) can never be deleted in mode 3: callers receive NotFound and the stale legacy row remains forever.

Mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy API state synchronously, racing the async legacy write

The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' subtest (line 132) and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtest (line 191) run the full doPlaylistTests suite, which checks legacy API state immediately after k8s writes — e.g. listing /api/playlists right after k8s Create and getFromBothAPIs right after k8s Update. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous (a goroutine with up to a 10s window), so these assertions race it and will flake: the legacy endpoint can still 404 or return the pre-update title. The mode-3 runs need eventually/polling-style assertions for legacy-side reads, or the legacy-side checks should be skipped for mode 3.

Storage create/update failures are recorded in the legacy-duration metric

When the unified-storage Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a legacy failure that never happened (legacy is never called on this path) into the legacy duration metric, with the storage start time, and never recording the actual storage failure. The same bug exists in Update at line 129. Both should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics that distinguish legacy vs unified errors.

Update passes raw UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy, so UpdatedObject runs twice and the two stores can diverge

Update now hands the raw rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update, meaning objInfo.UpdatedObject() is executed independently by each store against its own old object. The previous implementation resolved the object once (Storage.Get + UpdatedObject) and wrapped the result in updateWrapper so both stores persisted the identical object. With the new code, create-on-update paths that generate names/UIDs produce different objects in legacy vs unified storage, and any mutating logic inside UpdatedObject runs twice, so the two stores can silently hold divergent objects — exactly what dual write is meant to prevent. The object should be materialized once and the frozen result passed to the legacy update via updateWrapper, as before.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)

GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)

GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the data race this PR fixes

The PR adds a mutex to guard the package-level entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. A data-race fix without a test that exercises concurrent access can silently regress. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines against a temporary assets-manifest.json (with cfg.Env set to a non-dev value so the cache path is exercised) and is run with the race detector enabled (`go test -race`) would have caught the original race and would verify the fix going forward.

Write lock is held across manifest file I/O, serializing all GetWebAssets callers

The deferred Unlock at line 49 keeps entryPointAssetsCacheMu held while readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) opens, reads, and parses assets-manifest.json from disk. While the write lock is held, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks — including callers that would otherwise be served by the read-locked fast path, since RLock cannot proceed while the write lock is held. In dev mode (setting.Dev) the fast path is skipped by design, so every index page load now serializes on this disk I/O, and on a slow filesystem all such requests stall behind a single global mutex. Loading and parsing the manifest outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, leaving dead feature-flag logic and an unreachable SQL branch

The new enableSqlExpressions function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every path, so the feature-flag lookup is dead code and the entire `case QueryTypeSQL` body after the gate (lines 133-138) is unreachable. As written the code looks like a logic bug (an inverted check that is then discarded) and invites a future well-meaning 'fix' that flips it and silently re-enables the CVE-2024-9264 attack surface. If the intent is permanent removal, this should be an explicit `return false` (or an unconditional error at the call site) with a comment referencing the CVE; the accompanying user-facing message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is also misleading, since the feature is implemented but deliberately disabled for security reasons.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command path is blocked only implicitly via the stub DB error

The reader.go gate explicitly rejects QueryTypeSQL, but the legacy parsing path (UnmarshalSQLCommand -> NewSQLCommand, used by the rawNode-based query parsing) has no explicit disable check. It is blocked only as a side effect of sql.TablesList now always returning 'not implemented' from the stub DB, which surfaces to users as the confusing 400 error 'error reading SQL command' instead of a clear 'SQL expressions are disabled' message. Functionally this does close the hole today (and the DuckDB dependency is removed from go.mod), but the protection relies on the stub never being re-implemented; if pkg/expr/sql.DB is ever given a real implementation, this path would re-enable SQL expression execution with no feature-flag or security gate. An explicit check or comment here would make the security invariant robust against future refactoring.

No regression test for the CVE-2024-9264 fix

This PR disables SQL expressions to fix a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability but adds or updates no tests. There is no test asserting that a SQL expression query (e.g. one using read_csv/read_blob against a local file, the known exploit shape) is rejected through the ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery path, and none asserting that NewSQLCommand/sql.TablesList now fail. A future change that re-implements pkg/expr/sql.DB or touches the inverted logic in enableSqlExpressions could silently re-open the vulnerability without any test failing. Additionally, any existing unit tests that exercised sql.TablesList or SQLCommand against the real DuckDB are not touched in this PR and would now fail against the always-erroring stub, so the test suite state for this package should be verified.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the function-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration, which serialized builds; now nothing prevents two goroutines from building an index for the same NamespacedResource at the same time. This is reachable because getOrCreateIndex in pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go does GetIndex-then-BuildIndex with no per-key coordination (its own TODO admits this) — e.g. two concurrent Search gRPC requests for a namespace below InitMinCount, or a search racing a watch-event-driven build. Consequences: for file-backed indexes both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently (error or a corrupt/duplicated on-disk index), resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants is incremented twice, and the losing index is overwritten in b.cache without ever being closed, leaking the bleve index and its file handles. Consider a per-key mutex or singleflight so only one build per key runs and concurrent callers wait for it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex writes to the same map under b.cacheMu.Lock() (bleve.go:137-139) and GetIndex reads it under RLock. This PR adds a new caller in searchSupport.init (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go) that invokes s.search.TotalDocs() in the 'search index initialized' log line immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine; that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex for a not-yet-indexed namespace (handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> build). Concurrent map iteration and map insertion is a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error in Go ("concurrent map read and map write") and will crash the server. Fix: take b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the search watcher goroutine

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns without calling s.cancel() and without stopping whatever Init already started. The reordering in Init (search.init now runs before initWatcher) makes this concrete: if s.search.init(ctx) succeeds but s.initWatcher() then fails, search.init has already spawned a goroutine consuming WatchWriteEvents using context.Background() (search.go lines 202-213), which drives a DB poller every 100ms with no cancellation path. Previously initWatcher ran first, so its failure could not strand the search watcher. Call s.cancel() on the error path, and pass the server's cancellable context into the search watcher instead of context.Background() so it can actually be stopped.

Removing per-request Init checks also removes request rejection after Stop

The deleted `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards in every handler were also the mechanism that rejected traffic after shutdown: Stop() sets s.initErr ("service is stopping"/"service is stopped"), and each handler surfaced that error via s.Init. With the guards removed, a stopped server keeps serving Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search normally — only the internal watch context is cancelled — and the initErr writes in Stop() no longer have any effect on requests. If rejecting requests after Stop is still intended, add an explicit stopped check to the handlers; otherwise drop the now-dead initErr bookkeeping in Stop to avoid implying a guarantee that no longer exists.

Storage-server startup test disabled on postgres

This integration test is the one place exercising the PR's core change — initializing unified storage eagerly when the ResourceServer is constructed in the storage-server target — and the PR disables the postgres variant with a TODO. That leaves the new eager-init startup path (DB access plus index build during module init) without CI coverage on postgres, one of the two supported production databases, exactly when the startup behavior changed. If the failure indicates eager init breaks under postgres in some environments, skipping hides a real regression rather than a test-only problem; this should be root-caused or tracked before relying on the new startup behavior.

errgroup workers in init race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed

In searchSupport.init, each group.Go closure executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, writing to the err variable declared in the outer function scope, and also does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) without synchronization. Since this PR's goal is building many namespaces with high concurrency, these goroutines race: one worker can overwrite another worker's error between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait() can report nil even though a build failed — startup then proceeds with a missing or partial index for that namespace — and the unsynchronized counter increments corrupt the span attribute and will fail the Go race detector. Fix: use a closure-local variable (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and replace the counter with len(stats) or an atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup for literal alias "alias", so the ~21 created identity providers are never removed

In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup registered inside the provider-creation loops uses the literal string "alias": getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) (the same statement is repeated at line 425 for idp-alias-20). No provider with alias "alias" exists, so each cleanup call targets a non-existent resource (404) and, more importantly, the idp-alias-0 … idp-alias-20 providers created by the test are never cleaned up. That leaves over twenty stray brokers — eleven of them enabled, login-visible realm-level providers — in the test realm, which can skew any later test in the class or suite that lists or counts login identity providers. Capture the actual alias in an effectively-final variable and register cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove (note the same copy-pasted mistake already exists in testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303 and is worth fixing too).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update is computed against the org-aware wrapped model, so updates made while the org is disabled can leave stale login entries

In update(), the current state of the IDP is loaded via getById(model.getInternalId()), which returns the organization-aware wrapper produced by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled, deleted, or the OrganizationProvider is unavailable. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on this wrapped original: while the org is disabled, test(original) is always false, so the first early-return (!test(original) && !test(updated)) fires for any update that also makes the updated model fail the predicate — e.g. an admin sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or disables the raw IDP on a broker belonging to a disabled org. However, the .idp.login.* caches are populated from idpDelegate.getForLogin(), which only filters raw attributes (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, org-public) and does not consider org enabled state, so the raw-eligible IDP's id is still in the cached set and the needed invalidation is skipped. When the organization is later re-enabled nothing invalidates the login cache, getById resolves the stale id as enabled, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean — which only re-checks isEnabled() on the ORG_ONLY/ALL paths — will render a broker the admin explicitly hid from the login page. The 'original' used for the login predicate should be the unwrapped model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById(...)) so the predicate reflects raw stored attributes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore's JCA provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider

The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the "BouncyCastle security provider" (non-FIPS or FIPS). This implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. whatever provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically SUN), which is not BouncyCastle and varies with JDK configuration. The value is exposed via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER, which other Keycloak code uses as the provider name for JCA getInstance(algorithm, provider) lookups and which CryptoIntegration.init() logs as the "java security provider", so with this provider active those lookups resolve against an arbitrary default provider rather than the documented one. Each call also instantiates a KeyStore just to obtain a Provider. If no BouncyCastle is available, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or documenting the deviation would be more correct.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: two discarded ASN1Encoder instances in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder objects and write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them, but the results are never used — the returned DER sequence is built from fresh encoders in the return statement (lines 117-121). The two statements have no effect other than allocating throwaway objects and performing pointless serialization on every ES256/384/512 signature conversion, and they confuse readers about which encoders actually produce the output. They should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() on CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations

The PR adds `int order();` as a new abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` interface. keycloak-common is a published artifact and `CryptoProvider` is a ServiceLoader-loaded SPI that can be implemented outside this repository. Any existing compiled implementation used with the newer keycloak-common will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts via `CryptoProvider::order`, and any source implementation stops compiling until it implements the method. Declaring it as a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would provide the new ordering capability without breaking API/binary compatibility in a shared module.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
New test bypasses the ServiceLoader/order mechanism that is the point of the PR

The functional core of this PR is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider and is selected by CryptoIntegration only when no higher-order provider is present (DefaultCryptoProvider et al. use order 200, this one 100). The added test instantiates `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` directly, so a broken or missing service registration file, or an order() value that wins/loses incorrectly against DefaultCryptoProvider, would not be caught by anything. A test that loads providers through ServiceLoader/CryptoIntegration — e.g. asserting AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable on its own and that DefaultCryptoProvider still wins when both are on the classpath — would cover the mechanism the PR actually introduces.

Same-order crypto providers are now silently picked by classpath order instead of failing fast

detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath") whenever more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by order() and unconditionally takes the first entry. Because DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, a misconfigured classpath containing two of them — exactly the situation the old exception guarded against — no longer fails: one provider is silently chosen based on ServiceLoader/classpath ordering, which can vary between environments, and the only trace is a debug-level "Ignored crypto providers" message. In the worst case a deployment intended to run with the FIPS 140-2 provider boots with the default non-FIPS provider without anyone noticing. Consider keeping a hard failure, or at least logging a warning, when the highest order is shared by more than one provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission queries findByType("Clients") but per-client resources are created without a type

getClientsWithPermission iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to find per-client resources. However, per-client resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner) and setType is never called on them — only the all-type resources created in init() get a type (and removeOrphanResources discriminates per-object resources by name rather than type precisely because their type is unset). Since findByType matches on the resource's type column, per-client resources are never returned here: callers holding only per-client permissions get an empty set from partial client listing, and if the all-type resource matches, its name — the literal string "Clients", which is not a client id — is added to the returned set. Either set the resource type when creating per-client resources (V1 ClientPermissions.resource() sets type "kc.client.resource") or resolve per-client resource names from the permissions/policies the way the Users V2 flow does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the 'Clients' resource-type resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no per-client resource exists, the code does resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the schema is not supported for the realm (e.g., admin permissions disabled on the realm while the admin-permissions client still exists) and when the 'Clients' resource simply does not exist — which is the case for realms that enabled admin permissions before this change, because init() early-returns when the client already exists. The result is a NullPointerException and a 500 on ordinary admin operations such as viewing or updating a client for any caller without the manage-clients role. The sibling method hasPermission(String) correctly returns false when the resource is null; this path should do the same.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
No upgrade path: realms that already enabled admin permissions never receive the new Clients scopes and resource

init() creates the schema scopes and the all-type resources only when the admin-permissions client does not exist yet, and returns immediately if it does. Realms that enabled admin permissions (V2) before this change already have that client, so they never get the new scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) or the "Clients" resource-type resource. In such realms, creating a Clients permission fails in getOrCreateResource with ModelException("No scopes found.") when it looks up the missing scopes, and permission evaluation falls into the getResourceTypeResource() == null path in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission. A migration or repair step that adds newly introduced scopes and resource-type resources to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed.

UnsupportedOperationException in setPermissionsEnabled/isPermissionsEnabled breaks client deletion and the client management-permissions endpoint

ClientPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException from setPermissionsEnabled (line 193), isPermissionsEnabled (line 188), getPermissions, resource(), etc. These methods are reachable in normal operation: (1) AdminPermissions.registerListener handles ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). This PR makes MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() return ClientPermissionsV2, and the newly added Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) guard passes when V2 is enabled (the V2 feature pulls in V1), so every client removal on a server with the V2 feature enabled throws from the synchronous provider-event listener, rolling back the transaction — deleting a client fails with a 500 (and realm deletion, which removes all its clients, fails too). (2) The admin REST endpoint GET/PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions calls isPermissionsEnabled/getPermissions/setPermissionsEnabled (ClientResource's ManagementPermissionReference handling), so it now returns 500, breaking the admin console's client permissions handling under V2. Either implement these methods for V2 (e.g., on removal, clean up the client's FGAP resource and its policies) or make the listener and endpoints skip them gracefully. There is no test covering client deletion with the V2 feature enabled.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles lost the canManage(client) fallback, blocking manage-clients admins

In V1 ClientPermissions these methods are implemented as 'if (canManage(client)) return true; return hasPermission(...)'. The new V2 overrides only call hasPermission(client, MAP_ROLES / MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE) and drop the canManage short-circuit. Because AdminPermissions.evaluator returns MgmtPermissionsV2 for every realm when the V2 profile feature is enabled, an administrator holding the realm 'manage-clients' role — who can currently map client roles — will get 403 from the role-mapping endpoints (RoleMapperResource checks canMapRoles etc.) unless an explicit FGAP map-roles permission exists. It also breaks the intended transitivity that a MANAGE permission implies map-roles, which Users V2 explicitly supports (UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testTransitiveUserPermissions asserts role mapping works with only the manage scope; note canView(ClientScopeModel) in this same file does include MANAGE). The three overrides should include canManage(client) (or include the MANAGE scope in the evaluated scopes, as the Users V2 implementation does via varargs).

getResourceName has no Clients branch and returns null display names for Clients resources

getResourceName only resolves display names for the Users resource type and otherwise falls through to resource.getDisplayName(). Resources created for the admin-permissions schema (the all-type "Clients" resource and per-client resources) never have a display name set, so permission/resource representations for Clients resources come back with null names, and there is no "All clients" equivalent of the existing "All users" label. Add a CLIENTS branch that resolves the client (e.g., returning its clientId) for per-client resources and "All clients" for the type resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 silently repurposed from 'recreate upgrade required' to 'feature disabled'

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3, and 4 now means FEATURE_DISABLED. The update-compatibility tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and its exit codes are the supported contract for CI/CD pipelines. Any automation written against the previous preview that branches on exit code 4 to decide that a recreate upgrade is required will now misinterpret that case: a 'recreate required' result returns 3 (which such a script would treat as an unknown error), and a 'feature disabled' result returns 4 (which it would treat as 'recreate required', potentially triggering an unnecessary full shutdown and downtime). The docs table is updated in this PR, but existing scripts get no warning. If this renumbering is intentional, it should at least be called out in the release notes/upgrading guide so adopters of the preview can update their pipelines.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Caution overstates requirement: operator only fails when an update strategy is configured without the feature

The new CAUTION states 'the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail.' as a blanket statement. The PR's own UpgradeTest demonstrates otherwise: createInitialDeployment returns early without enabling the feature when no update strategy is set (updateStrategy == null), and that deployment is expected to become ready and to handle an image change with the default recreate behavior. The feature is only required when spec.update.strategy is configured on the Keycloak CR. As written, users who never set an update strategy will be told they must enable a preview feature to keep the Operator from failing, which is not true. Reword to scope the requirement, e.g. 'When spec.update.strategy is configured, the preview feature rolling-updates must be enabled; otherwise the Operator will fail to process the update.'

Feature-disabled path tested only for 'metadata' and documented exit code 4 never asserted

The new testFeatureNotEnabled only launches 'update-compatibility metadata' and asserts only the stderr message. The check subcommand's feature-disabled branch (UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run) has no coverage, and neither test asserts the exit code, even though the documentation added in this PR advertises exit code 4 ('The feature rolling-updates is disabled') as part of the scripting contract. A regression where picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) returns the wrong code (e.g., 0 or 1) would silently break the automation contract this PR documents. Add a feature-disabled test for 'check' and assert exitCode() == 4 in both tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage rights to admins holding only the 'view' scope on groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), and hasPermission returns true when ANY of the listed scopes is granted. canManage()/requireManage() is the guard for GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups), so an administrator who was granted only the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type (no manage-users role, no manage scope) can create arbitrary top-level groups. The per-group counterpart canManage(GroupModel) in the same class correctly checks only MANAGE, and the Users V2 equivalent only checks the manage scope, so including VIEW here is a privilege escalation, not intended semantics. The new javadoc on GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() also documents the wrong behavior. The VIEW scope should be removed from this check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses resource type/id incorrectly and returns wrong identifiers

This method is broken in three compounding ways. (1) It iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...), but per-group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource never have resource.setType() called (only the all-groups resource created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init() has a type), so specific group resources are never visited. (2) Inside the loop it calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...), but hasPermission looks resources up by NAME via resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), so passing the resource UUID never finds the resource and the check silently falls back to the all-groups resource for every entry. (3) It adds groupResource.getId() (the authz resource UUID) to the result, while all callers (UsersResource.searchForUser, UsersResource.getUsersCount, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser) need actual group IDs to restrict the user query via the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute. Consequences: an admin whose only access is view-members/manage-members on specific groups gets an empty set, so the DB-level group filter is never applied and /users/count returns 0 while pagination is computed on unfiltered results; and an admin granted view-members on the all-groups resource gets a set containing a non-existent 'group id' (the resource UUID), so the user search is restricted to a group that doesn't exist and returns zero users.

false_positives.candidate:
Null 'Groups' type resource is dereferenced; no upgrade path creates it for realms that already enabled admin permissions

In hasPermission(), when no per-group resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, "Groups") and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).getId() semantics — getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource server has no resource named "Groups", and findByResource(server, null) NPEs inside the store, producing a 500 on any group admin endpoint (group list, view, manage checks). This state is reachable for any realm that enabled admin permissions (realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null) before this change was deployed: AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when the client already exists, and nothing in this PR migrates existing resource servers to add the new "Groups" resource or the manage-members/view-members/manage-membership scopes. Those realms also cannot create group permissions, since getScope() validation fails for the missing scopes. A null guard plus an upgrade/initialization path for existing resource servers is needed.

setPermissionsEnabled() throws UnsupportedOperationException but is still invoked by the GroupRemovedEvent listener

Because MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() now returns GroupPermissionsV2, any caller of the GroupPermissionManagement methods hits UnsupportedOperationException. One such caller runs on the normal group-deletion path: AdminPermissions.registerListener registers a ProviderEventListener whenever Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled (enabling the V2 feature also enables V1), and on every GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent it calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false). With V2 enabled that call now throws, so deleting a group (DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}, which fires GroupRemovedEvent synchronously via realm.removeGroup) fails with a 500 instead of completing. The same problem affects GroupResource's management/permissions endpoints, which call permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group)/setPermissionsEnabled(...) after ProfileHelper.requireFeature(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) — that check passes under V2, so those endpoints also 500. The V2 overrides should no-op (as the V1 implementation effectively does when no V1 resources exist) rather than throw.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).

Lithuanian users will now see an Italian sentence on the OTP setup page of the account console. true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.

Traditional Chinese text introduced into the Simplified Chinese (zh_CN) account bundle

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor validation requires identical anchors in identical order and stops at the first mismatch

In `santizeAnchors` the n-th anchor found in the translation is compared with the n-th anchor found in the English source using sequential `find()` calls. A translation that contains exactly the same anchors as the source but in a different order — legitimate when grammar or right-to-left mirroring reorders links in a sentence — is reported as "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string" and fails the build. Italian text inserted into the Lithuanian login messages (loginTotpStep1)

`loginTotpStep1` was changed from a Lithuanian sentence to "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian. Lithuanian users will see Italian text in the mobile authenticator setup step of the login flow. true_positives.matched_candidate:

The PR adds `int order();` as a new abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` interface. keycloak-common is a published artifact and `CryptoProvider` is a ServiceLoader-loaded SPI that can be implemented outside this repository. Any existing compiled implementation used with the newer keycloak-common will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts via `CryptoProvider::order`, and any source implementation stops compiling until it implements the method. false_positives.candidate:
Same-order crypto providers are now silently picked by classpath order instead of failing fast

detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath") whenever more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by order() and unconditionally takes the first entry. Because DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, a misconfigured classpath containing two of them — exactly the situation the old exception guarded against — no longer fails: one provider is silently chosen based on ServiceLoader/classpath ordering, which can vary between environments, and the only trace is a debug-level "Ignored crypto providers" message. In the worst case a deployment intended to run with the FIPS 140-2 provider boots with the default non-FIPS provider without anyone noticing. Consider keeping a hard failure, or at least logging a warning, when the highest order is shared by more than one provider.

New test bypasses the ServiceLoader/order mechanism that is the point of the PR

The functional core of this PR is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider and is selected by CryptoIntegration only when no higher-order provider is present (DefaultCryptoProvider et al. use order 200, this one 100). The added test instantiates `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` directly, so a broken or missing service registration file, or an order() value that wins/loses incorrectly against DefaultCryptoProvider, would not be caught by anything. A test that loads providers through ServiceLoader/CryptoIntegration — e.g. asserting AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable on its own and that DefaultCryptoProvider still wins when both are on the classpath — would cover the mechanism the PR actually introduces.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance guard makes kill()/terminate() dead code for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

The check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is never true in practice. Flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances; `SpawnProcess` is a sibling of `multiprocessing.context.Process` (both subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`), not a subclass of it, and the only alternative type here is `threading.Thread`, which also fails the check. Consequences: (1) when a flusher process is detected as hung (cause == "hang"), the old process is never killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement, so two processes end up flushing the same shards and producing the same segments to the buffered-segments topic (duplicate downstream data), and each restart leaks the previous process's Redis/Kafka connections; the old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implementation and is timing-dependent

In test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, the final assertion (assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets) contradicts the code under test: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes offsets in a finally block even when the result processor raises, so both submitted offsets (100 and 101) become committable and the background commit loop (1s cadence) will commit them. The test only passes when the assertion executes before the commit thread's first tick (~1s after create_with_partitions); on a slow or loaded CI worker it will fail intermittently. The assertion also contradicts the test's own docstring ('errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages'), which implies the successful second message's offset should eventually be committed.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down on the first rebalance; all later messages are silently dropped but their offsets committed

FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is passed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_with_partitions. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which calls shutdown() on each internal queue.Queue. After the first rebalance the factory hands the already-shut-down pool to the new strategy: FixedQueuePool.submit's work_queue.put(...) raises queue.ShutDown, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and then marks the message's offset as completed, so the background commit thread commits offsets for messages that were never processed. Net effect: after any rebalance (deploy, scaling, partition movement) the consumer silently drops every subsequent message while advancing committed offsets — silent data loss plus one exception log per message — until the process is restarted. The shared OffsetTracker also retains state for revoked partitions, so the new commit thread will attempt to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or close() should not shut down a factory-owned pool), and a rebalance test is missing.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit when processing lags

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so put() never blocks and queued work is unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit is called synchronously from the StreamProcessor poll loop, meaning that when processing is slower than intake — the exact scenario this PR is designed to mitigate — messages are continuously pulled from Kafka and accumulated in memory, growing consumer RSS until OOM and inflating consumer lag. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false with unbounded queues. Use bounded queues (a blocking put naturally throttles the poll loop) or pause consumption when queue depth exceeds a threshold.

A single permanent offset gap wedges all future commits for a partition and the per-second scan grows unboundedly

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets only advances the committable offset through a strictly contiguous integer range (for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)). Any permanent gap in a partition's offsets blocks commits for that partition forever: Kafka topics written by transactional producers contain control-record batches that consume offsets without ever being delivered to the consumer, and compacted topics have gaps by design. Once wedged, the committed offset never advances, so every restart replays the entire post-gap backlog, and the commit loop re-scans range(start, max_offset + 1) every second, growing by one iteration per new message and burning ever-increasing CPU in the commit thread. The new tests (test_offset_gaps_block_commits) enshrine gap-blocking as intended, but it does not match Kafka offset semantics; iterating over sorted(all_offsets) and blocking only on seen-but-still-outstanding offsets would handle gaps without losing safety for submitted-but-unfinished work.

Shutdown stops the commit thread before workers finish; final completed offsets are never committed and queued work is dropped

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the background commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any offsets that workers complete after the commit thread exits (in-flight items at shutdown — common here since this mode targets slow items) are never committed and will be reprocessed on restart. Additionally, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so each worker exits after finishing only its current item and all remaining queued items are discarded rather than drained, despite the 'gracefully shutdown' docstring (their offsets stay uncommitted, so this is reprocessing rather than loss, but it discards the backlog on every deploy/rebalance). Finally, join(timeout) ignores its timeout argument and just calls close() again, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each of the N workers with its own 5s timeout, so strategy shutdown can take up to ~5*N seconds (default N=20 → ~100s) regardless of the join_timeout the StreamProcessor requested.

test_stats_reporting races with live worker threads and can flake on total_items > 0

In TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 work items and then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 while three real worker threads (started in setUp) are actively draining the queues. If the main thread is preempted during the submit loop (e.g., on a loaded CI machine), the workers can process all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making total_items 0 and failing the assertion intermittently. The test should block processing (e.g., with a threading.Event the result processor waits on) before asserting a nonzero queue depth.
