Advanced negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative index, which Django rejects

When enable_advanced_features is set and the incoming cursor has a negative offset — trivially supplied by a client as cursor=0:-5:0, which Cursor.from_string parses without any validation — the branch at lines 877-882 executes queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra] with a negative start index. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing/slicing by raising ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported."), so the comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false and this request crashes with an unhandled 500. The endpoint in organization_auditlogs.py enables this path for superusers/global-access members who pass optimized_pagination=true, so any such caller supplying a negative-offset cursor gets a server error instead of the advertised "efficient reverse pagination."
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py applies negative slice offsets to a Django QuerySet, which Django rejects. The differing exception type does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

organization_context.member may be None; unconditional .has_global_access dereference can 500 every audit log request

RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is Optional — it is None when the caller can access the organization without holding a membership, e.g. requests authenticated with an organization auth token, where request.user is anonymous and is_superuser is False. For those callers the short-circuit on request.user.is_superuser does not protect the second operand, and evaluating organization_context.member.has_global_access raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'. Because this line executes unconditionally for every GET (not only when optimized_pagination=true), it turns previously working requests into 500s. It should be guarded (e.g. organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access), and it should be verified that has_global_access exists on the RpcOrganizationMember pydantic model, not only on the ORM OrganizationMember.

The candidate's broader claim about all GET requests and additional model concern do not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator applies numeric key math to a datetime column and 500s on every non-empty page

The audit log endpoint invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key and value_from_cursor were copied from the numeric Paginator instead of DateTimePaginator. get_item_key executes math.ceil(getattr(item, "datetime")), which raises TypeError ("must be real number, not datetime.datetime") because datetime objects have no float conversion. build_cursor calls get_item_key whenever a page has at least one result (to compute the next/prev cursor values), so any request with optimized_pagination=true against an organization that has at least one audit log entry fails with an unhandled 500. Even if that were fixed, value_from_cursor returns the raw millisecond cursor value, which build_queryset then compares directly against the timestamp column in SQL (datetime_col <= <bigint>) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so page 2 and beyond would return wrong data or a database error. The class should subclass DateTimePaginator or reuse its get_item_key/value_from_cursor implementations.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: the audit logs paginator orders by datetime, but get_item_key applies numeric math.ceil/math.floor to datetime objects, causing a TypeError. Its additional cursor-decoding concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
New paginator and audit-log pagination path ship with no tests

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator (about 90 lines duplicating BasePaginator.get_result) plus a new branch in the organization audit logs endpoint, but adds no tests for either. A single smoke test calling the endpoint with optimized_pagination=true against an org containing one audit log entry would have caught that get_item_key crashes on datetime values (paginator.py:840), and a negative-offset test would have caught the invalid queryset slicing (paginator.py:882). Since this paginator is documented as intended for reuse on high-traffic endpoints, it needs coverage for the first page, next/prev pages with datetime cursors, and negative offsets before merging.

Comment claims BasePaginator now allows negative offsets, but the code clamps them to 0

The added comment in BasePaginator.get_result says the change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning," but the code does the opposite for forward cursors: start_offset = max(0, offset) clamps any negative offset to 0, and for previous-page cursors the behavior is identical to before (the offset is passed through unchanged). The change is therefore a behavior-preserving clamp, not the optimization described, and the misleading text (echoed by the comment added in cursors.py:26-27) may lead future callers to believe negative offsets are safely supported here, when any negative value that actually reaches a queryset slice raises ValueError.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the function-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration, which serialized builds; now nothing prevents two goroutines from building an index for the same NamespacedResource at the same time. This is reachable because getOrCreateIndex in pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go does GetIndex-then-BuildIndex with no per-key coordination (its own TODO admits this) — e.g. two concurrent Search gRPC requests for a namespace below InitMinCount, or a search racing a watch-event-driven build. Consequences: for file-backed indexes both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory concurrently (error or a corrupt/duplicated on-disk index), resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants is incremented twice, and the losing index is overwritten in b.cache without ever being closed, leaking the bleve index and its file handles. Consider a per-key mutex or singleflight so only one build per key runs and concurrent callers wait for it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: removing the function-wide cacheMu lock permits multiple goroutines to build the same index concurrently for the same key, with locking limited to cache assignment. Its additional consequences and mitigation suggestions do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex writes to the same map under b.cacheMu.Lock() (bleve.go:137-139) and GetIndex reads it under RLock. This PR adds a new caller in searchSupport.init (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go) that invokes s.search.TotalDocs() in the 'search index initialized' log line immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine; that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex for a not-yet-indexed namespace (handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> build). Concurrent map iteration and map insertion is a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error in Go ("concurrent map read and map write") and will crash the server. Fix: take b.cacheMu.RLock() around the iteration in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with BuildIndex writes triggered by the newly started event watcher, potentially causing a concurrent map access panic.

false_positives.candidate:
errgroup workers in init race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed

In searchSupport.init, each group.Go closure executes `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, writing to the err variable declared in the outer function scope, and also does `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) without synchronization. Since this PR's goal is building many namespaces with high concurrency, these goroutines race: one worker can overwrite another worker's error between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait() can report nil even though a build failed — startup then proceeds with a missing or partial index for that namespace — and the unsynchronized counter increments corrupt the span attribute and will fail the Go race detector. Fix: use a closure-local variable (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and replace the counter with len(stats) or an atomic.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the search watcher goroutine

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns without calling s.cancel() and without stopping whatever Init already started. The reordering in Init (search.init now runs before initWatcher) makes this concrete: if s.search.init(ctx) succeeds but s.initWatcher() then fails, search.init has already spawned a goroutine consuming WatchWriteEvents using context.Background() (search.go lines 202-213), which drives a DB poller every 100ms with no cancellation path. Previously initWatcher ran first, so its failure could not strand the search watcher. Call s.cancel() on the error path, and pass the server's cancellable context into the search watcher instead of context.Background() so it can actually be stopped.

Removing per-request Init checks also removes request rejection after Stop

The deleted `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }` guards in every handler were also the mechanism that rejected traffic after shutdown: Stop() sets s.initErr ("service is stopping"/"service is stopped"), and each handler surfaced that error via s.Init. With the guards removed, a stopped server keeps serving Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search normally — only the internal watch context is cancelled — and the initErr writes in Stop() no longer have any effect on requests. If rejecting requests after Stop is still intended, add an explicit stopped check to the handlers; otherwise drop the now-dead initErr bookkeeping in Stop to avoid implying a guarantee that no longer exists.

Storage-server startup test disabled on postgres

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down on the first rebalance; all later messages are silently dropped but their offsets committed

FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is passed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_with_partitions. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which calls shutdown() on each internal queue.Queue. After the first rebalance the factory hands the already-shut-down pool to the new strategy: FixedQueuePool.submit's work_queue.put(...) raises queue.ShutDown, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and then marks the message's offset as completed, so the background commit thread commits offsets for messages that were never processed. Net effect: after any rebalance (deploy, scaling, partition movement) the consumer silently drops every subsequent message while advancing committed offsets — silent data loss plus one exception log per message — until the process is restarted. The shared OffsetTracker also retains state for revoked partitions, so the new commit thread will attempt to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or close() should not shut down a factory-owned pool), and a rebalance test is missing.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit when processing lags

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so put() never blocks and queued work is unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit is called synchronously from the StreamProcessor poll loop, meaning that when processing is slower than intake — the exact scenario this PR is designed to mitigate — messages are continuously pulled from Kafka and accumulated in memory, growing consumer RSS until OOM and inflating consumer lag. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false with unbounded queues. Use bounded queues (a blocking put naturally throttles the poll loop) or pause consumption when queue depth exceeds a threshold.

A single permanent offset gap wedges all future commits for a partition and the per-second scan grows unboundedly

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets only advances the committable offset through a strictly contiguous integer range (for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)). Any permanent gap in a partition's offsets blocks commits for that partition forever: Kafka topics written by transactional producers contain control-record batches that consume offsets without ever being delivered to the consumer, and compacted topics have gaps by design. Once wedged, the committed offset never advances, so every restart replays the entire post-gap backlog, and the commit loop re-scans range(start, max_offset + 1) every second, growing by one iteration per new message and burning ever-increasing CPU in the commit thread. The new tests (test_offset_gaps_block_commits) enshrine gap-blocking as intended, but it does not match Kafka offset semantics; iterating over sorted(all_offsets) and blocking only on seen-but-still-outstanding offsets would handle gaps without losing safety for submitted-but-unfinished work.

Shutdown stops the commit thread before workers finish; final completed offsets are never committed and queued work is dropped

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the background commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any offsets that workers complete after the commit thread exits (in-flight items at shutdown — common here since this mode targets slow items) are never committed and will be reprocessed on restart. Additionally, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so each worker exits after finishing only its current item and all remaining queued items are discarded rather than drained, despite the 'gracefully shutdown' docstring (their offsets stay uncommitted, so this is reprocessing rather than loss, but it discards the backlog on every deploy/rebalance). Finally, join(timeout) ignores its timeout argument and just calls close() again, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each of the N workers with its own 5s timeout, so strategy shutdown can take up to ~5*N seconds (default N=20 → ~100s) regardless of the join_timeout the StreamProcessor requested.

test_stats_reporting races with live worker threads and can flake on total_items > 0

In TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 work items and then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 while three real worker threads (started in setUp) are actively draining the queues. If the main thread is preempted during the submit loop (e.g., on a loaded CI machine), the workers can process all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making total_items 0 and failing the assertion intermittently. The test should block processing (e.g., with a threading.Event the result processor waits on) before asserting a nonzero queue depth.

The PR changes the value type of the existing span-buf:s:* keys from a Redis SET (SADD here, SUNIONSTORE/SCARD/SSCAN elsewhere) to a sorted set (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data) without renaming the keys. Since the score is only used for eviction ordering, duplicated spans are subsequently treated as the newest spans and are evicted last by the 1000-span cap below, skewing eviction and, with repeated duplicates, crowding out legitimate spans. Add 'AGGREGATE MAX' (or MIN) to both ZUNIONSTORE calls so scores stay idempotent.

The test changes only add the new required end_timestamp_precise field to Span constructors. true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration row has `sender` in its metadata. That is not true: `build_integration` only stores `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is set, and integrations created through the normal in-Sentry pipeline never have it (the PR's own test_basic_flow asserts the final metadata contains only access_token/expires_at/icon/domain_name/account_type). Only integrations created by the installation webhook carry `sender`. This code path is reachable whenever an ACTIVE Integration exists with no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. the owning organization was deleted, orphaning the Integration row — and someone then installs the same GitHub App installation into another Sentry organization. In that case `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended github-integration-failed.html page, with no way to complete the install. false_positives.candidate:

OAuthLoginView.dispatch performs two outbound HTTP calls that can raise: `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) is outside the try/except (the try only covers safe_urlread/parsing), and `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) has no exception handling at all. A DNS/connection failure or timeout to github.com, or a non-JSON error body from the api.github.com/user call (resp.json() raises), will propagate out of the pipeline and return a 500 to the user, instead of the graceful github-integration-failed.html error page this PR introduces for every other verification failure. These calls should be wrapped and converted into the same error response (ideally with logging), since transient GitHub/network errors in a user-facing auth pipeline are expected.

Fresh-install path performs no verification that the OAuth user controls the installation

When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` and `build_integration` fetches `/app/installations/{installation_id}` using the GitHub App JWT — which can read ANY installation of the Sentry GitHub App. GitHub App installation IDs are sequential/enumerable, and the OAuth step only proves the attacker's own GitHub identity; on this path it is never compared to anything about the installation. So if the Integration row does not exist yet — the installation.created webhook is delayed, permanently failed to deliver, or webhooks aren't configured/reachable (self-hosted) — anyone who knows or guesses a victim's installation_id can attach the victim's GitHub organization installation to their own Sentry organization, exposing its repositories, commits, CODEOWNERS and source-linking data. The sender check added here only helps once the webhook-created row exists. Consider additionally verifying on the fresh path that the authenticated GitHub user belongs to / admins the installation's account (e.g. via the installation account and an org-membership check), rather than skipping verification entirely.

GitHub integration install now hard-requires the github-login OAuth app to be configured

OAuthLoginView pulls `client_id`/`client_secret` from GitHubIdentityProvider (the github-login identity OAuth app, e.g. the `github-login.client-id`/`github-login.client-secret` options), which is a separate configuration from the GitHub App (github-app.* options) that the integration previously needed. On deployments that have the GitHub App configured but never set up the github-login identity provider (a plausible self-hosted configuration), these values are None/empty: the pipeline will redirect to GitHub's authorize URL with an invalid client_id (GitHub shows an error) or the token exchange will fail, making the GitHub integration uninstallable where it previously worked. There is no feature flag, fallback, or documentation noting this new requirement. Consider gating the new step on the OAuth app being configured, or explicitly failing with a clear operator-facing error/docs update.

No positive-path test for the sender-match flow, and no test for integrations missing sender metadata

The new tests only cover the negative case (test_github_user_mismatch: webhook-created Integration whose sender does not match the OAuth user). There is no test that exercises the main protected flow end-to-end: installation webhook creates the Integration with a sender, the same GitHub user completes the OAuth step, the sender check passes, and the installation links successfully (the direct-from-GitHub install path). A regression that breaks legitimate installs from GitHub would not be caught. There is also no test with a pre-existing ACTIVE Integration whose metadata lacks `sender`, which would have exposed the KeyError in `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` reported separately.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)

GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incomplete double-checked locking bug in GetWebAssets: the cache is checked under a read lock but not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate focuses on the missing second cache check, it explicitly identifies the golden issue: a failed fetch can overwrite an already-valid cache entry with nil. This is a semantic match for the cache-corruption bug.

false_positives.candidate:

The deferred Unlock at line 49 keeps entryPointAssetsCacheMu held while readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) opens, reads, and parses assets-manifest.json from disk. While the write lock is held, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks — including callers that would otherwise be served by the read-locked fast path, since RLock cannot proceed while the write lock is held. In dev mode (setting.Dev) the fast path is skipped by design, so every index page load now serializes on this disk I/O, and on a slow filesystem all such requests stall behind a single global mutex. Loading and parsing the manifest outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid this.

The PR adds a mutex to guard the package-level entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. A data-race fix without a test that exercises concurrent access can silently regress. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines against a temporary assets-manifest.json (with cfg.Env set to a non-dev value so the cache path is exercised) and is run with the race detector enabled (`go test -race`) would have caught the original race and would verify the fix going forward.

On other databases the batch size is configurable and unvalidated: if it is set above the driver's bind-parameter cap (65535 for Postgres, and MySQL prepared statements have a similar 65535 placeholder limit), every cleanup batch will fail with a parameter-count error, so cleanup never makes progress. In the SQLite branch of deleteByIDs the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n^2) work. With the batch size this path is designed for (e.g. 32767 IDs, as exercised by the new test), that is on the order of gigabytes of byte copying per batch, repeated on every cleanup cycle while a backlog exists. Using a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-formatted values) would make it linear.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the asynchronous legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is created with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), deriving from the incoming request context. In the Kubernetes API server the request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write completes. The detached goroutine therefore almost always executes with an already-canceled context and the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' — in mode 3 the legacy copy (the stated 'safe measure') is silently skipped, with only a metric recording the failure. The goroutine should first detach values from the request lifecycle, e.g. ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the 10s timeout.

Update now hands the raw rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update, meaning objInfo.UpdatedObject() is executed independently by each store against its own old object. The previous implementation resolved the object once (Storage.Get + UpdatedObject) and wrapped the result in updateWrapper so both stores persisted the identical object. With the new code, create-on-update paths that generate names/UIDs produce different objects in legacy vs unified storage, and any mutating logic inside UpdatedObject runs twice, so the two stores can silently hold divergent objects — exactly what dual write is meant to prevent. The object should be materialized once and the frozen result passed to the legacy update via updateWrapper, as before.

Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy-only objects can never be deleted

Delete now returns immediately on any error from unified storage, including NotFound. The previous implementation special-cased apierrors.IsNotFound and still issued the legacy delete. With the new early return, an object that exists only in legacy storage (created before unified storage was enabled, or left behind by a failed dual write) can never be deleted in mode 3: callers receive NotFound and the stale legacy row remains forever.

The mode-3 runs need eventually/polling-style assertions for legacy-side reads, or the legacy-side checks should be skipped for mode 3.

When the unified-storage Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a legacy failure that never happened (legacy is never called on this path) into the legacy duration metric, with the storage start time, and never recording the actual storage failure. The comment now describes behavior that no longer exists and is misleading about what the remaining upsertQueryData does; update the comment and rename the variable.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting defeats the $__range no-splitting guard

runSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 299) before partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query)) runs on the next line. applyTemplateVariables substitutes the built-in range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from scopedVars, and dashboard/Explore requests always carry those scoped vars. querySupportsSplitting() decides a query must not be split by calling isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr), which searches for the literal text '$__range' — but by the time it runs, that text has already been replaced (e.g. count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) has become count_over_time({a="b"}[30d])). Consequence: queries using $__range are now time-split instead of being routed to nonSplittingQueries and executed once over the full range, which is exactly what the comment above the check says must not happen. Besides contradicting the documented intent, this is a real cost/correctness regression for large ranges: with a 30-day dashboard, each 1-day chunk evaluates count_over_time(...[30d]), re-scanning ~30 days of data per chunk (~30x the scanned volume of the previous single request). The existing unit tests do not catch this because the test requests carry no scopedVars, so $__range survives interpolation in tests but not in production. The isQueryWithRangeVariable check should run on the raw, pre-interpolation expr — or, if splitting such queries is now intentional, the dead check and its misleading comment should be removed.

Queries are now interpolated two to three times (runShardSplitQuery / runSplitQuery / runQuery)

Interpolation is now applied repeatedly to the same targets. LokiDatasource.runQuery — which the splitting code calls for every sub-request (runSplitGroupedQueries in querySplitting.ts, and splitQueriesByStreamShard here) — already maps targets through applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). With the new .map(...) added here in runShardSplitQuery and the one added in runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts), every sub-query in the time-splitting path is interpolated twice, and every sub-query in the shard-splitting path three times (runShardSplitQuery → runSplitQuery → runQuery), because sub-requests keep the original request.scopedVars and request.filters. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters from request.filters are injected into the stream selector on every pass, so the LogQL selectors sent to Loki contain each ad hoc matcher two or three times (previously they were injected exactly once, in runQuery); (2) any variable value that itself contains template syntax (a constant/text variable holding a literal containing another variable's name, or a $-prefixed token) is interpolated again by the later passes, silently altering the query Loki executes. The updated shard-splitting test that expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single-target request (1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 1 per shard group in runSplitQuery, with runQuery mocked) shows the redundancy is being baked into the tests rather than eliminated. One of the interpolation layers should be removed (or the later passes skipped for already-interpolated targets).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-act race between CountDevices and the insert allows exceeding the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first calling CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT/upsert. The count and the insert are separate, non-transactional queries. Two concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the anon_device table ends up with more devices than the configured limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (e.g., a public dashboard link being opened by many clients at once, or multiple Grafana HA replicas), the limit is only a soft cap. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a single statement with a subquery guard, a transaction with appropriate isolation, or an INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-act race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check before inserting, causing the configured device limit to be exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed on retry because the local cache is populated before the store write succeeds

In tagDeviceUI, the device cache key is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) at line 87) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first request from a new device is correctly rejected in the anonymous auth client (client.go returns the error). However, the cache entry remains for ~29 minutes (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)). Any subsequent request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the store, and the anonymous authentication succeeds. The consequence is that the new configurable device limit is effectively unenforced: a blocked device only sees one failed request and then gets full anonymous access by simply retrying (e.g., refreshing the browser), with the block re-asserting only once per 29-minute cache-expiry window. The cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (or the key must be removed when it returns an error).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the cache entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing retries to bypass the device limit until the 29-minute cache expiry.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved from background goroutine into the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and a recover() guard, so anonymous authentication never blocked on the database write and a panic in tagging could not affect the request. This PR calls TagDevice synchronously in Authenticate for all deployments, including the default case where device_limit is unset (0) and the enforcement is not needed. On every local-cache miss (roughly once per 29 minutes per device) each anonymous request now waits for the COUNT + upsert round trips before an identity is returned, and a panic in the tagging path now propagates into request handling. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when the limit is disabled, or restoring the timeout/recover protection.

No test for the allowed path (existing device updated when limit is reached) or for repeated rejection

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a brand-new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is hit. Two important behaviors are untested: (1) that a device already present in anon_device is still successfully updated (updateDevice returns nil) when count >= deviceLimit — this is the intended happy path that keeps existing devices working, and a regression there would lock out legitimate users; (2) that a rejected device keeps being rejected on subsequent TagDevice/CreateOrUpdateDevice attempts — a test through AnonDeviceService.TagDevice would have caught the local-cache bypass where the second request from a blocked device succeeds.

New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini

The PR introduces cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from key 'device_limit' in the [auth.anonymous] section, but it does not add the option to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where the other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented with comments. As shipped, the setting is undiscoverable for administrators and its semantics (0 = unlimited, limit counted over devices active in the last 30 days) are undocumented.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation LRU cache key ignores the site-specific fallback locale

The cache key for memoized translations is built only from the key, the current locale and the backend object id (`k = "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`). With this PR, the resolved value of a translation now also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (via `FallbackLocaleList`), and that setting is per-site on multisite installs and can be changed at runtime — but it is not part of the cache key, and the cache itself (`@cache` on the I18n singleton) is process-global. Consequences: (1) on a multisite cluster sharing one process, a key missing in locale X is resolved through whichever site's default locale populated the cache first — e.g. a user on a site whose default is German can be served the French fallback string cached for another site, until the 300-entry LRU happens to evict it; (2) on a single site, after an admin changes `default_locale`, fallback strings in the old language keep being served from the cache until eviction. Previously (`config.i18n.fallbacks = true`) the fallback target was the global `I18n.default_locale`, so cached entries were consistent. Include `SiteSetting.default_locale` (or the resolved fallback chain) in the cache key, or clear `I18n`'s cache when the setting changes.

Fallback locale files are only loaded for controller requests, so fallbacks silently fail in jobs/mailers/rake

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from the `set_locale` before_filter, i.e. only for HTTP requests through ApplicationController. The translate accelerator's `translate` only ever loads yml files for `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)`); it never loads the fallback locales itself. Any server-side code that translates outside a web request — Sidekiq jobs, ActionMailer views, rake tasks, console — with `I18n.locale` set to a non-English locale will walk the fallback chain (locale → site default → :en), find that no translations were ever loaded for the fallback locales, and render "translation missing: xx.yyy" instead of the site-default/English string. So the feature this PR adds silently does not work in exactly the server-side contexts that don't pass through a controller. Load the fallback locales inside the accelerator instead (e.g. have `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`translate` load every locale in `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`), or route jobs/mailers through the same ensure_loaded! step.

FallbackLocaleList#[] does a SiteSetting read and several array allocations on every interpolated translation

The i18n fallbacks backend calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every backend lookup, and `FallbackLocaleList#[]` performs a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read plus `[locale, ...].uniq.compact` (multiple array allocations) each time. The translate accelerator only memoizes argument-free lookups — every `I18n.t` call with interpolation options (the common case in this codebase, e.g. anything with `count:` or a username) bypasses the LRU cache and pays this cost per call, in a code path that exists specifically to make translation fast. Consider memoizing the computed list keyed by (locale, default_locale) and invalidating when the setting changes.

No tests for the new fallback semantics, which now apply to all environments

This PR rewrites how fallbacks are computed (new `FallbackLocaleList`, new `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, per-request `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`) and, as a side effect, enables fallbacks in every environment — previously they were only turned on via `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in the production-like configs, so in development/test a key present in English but missing in the active locale now silently renders the English text instead of a "translation missing" message. No specs cover any of this. At minimum, add coverage that `I18n.fallbacks[:xx]` returns `[xx, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq`, that a key missing in the active locale resolves through the site default and then English, and that the fallback locale files are actually loaded (the `ensure_loaded!` path).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

traceID field dropped from "Plugin Request Completed" log lines

Before this change, LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended a "traceID" field to every "Plugin Request Completed" log line via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false). This PR removes that code (and the tracing import) and relies entirely on contextual attributes attached by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware — but instrumentContext in contextual_logger_middleware.go only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it never adds traceID. This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh instance, so logs via FromContext are never recorded

This matters because the production code changed in this PR (LoggerMiddleware) now logs exclusively through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...). Any test that injects a *TestLogger and then asserts on InfoLogs/ErrorLogs/etc. of the instance it holds will see zero recorded calls — tests expecting a log will fail confusingly, and tests asserting that nothing was logged will silently false-pass even though the code under test did log. The fake should return f (or record into shared state) so that logs written through FromContext are observable by the test.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver, causing logs to be recorded on a separate instance and breaking assertions on the original test logger.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running earlier in the chain

LoggerMiddleware previously built the pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, and dsUID log fields itself from req.PluginContext, so it was self-contained. After this change those fields only appear if ContextualLoggerMiddleware ran earlier in the middleware stack and attached them as contextual attributes. The production wiring in CreateMiddlewares happens to order them correctly, but NewLoggerMiddleware is exported and can be composed into other middleware stacks (tests, other decorator constructions); in any stack without ContextualLoggerMiddleware ahead of it, the "Plugin Request Completed" lines lose all plugin-identifying fields with no error or warning. New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test, and no test covers the moved log fields

The PR adds a new middleware (ContextualLoggerMiddleware) responsible for attaching endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname to the request context, but adds no test verifying those attributes are attached, and the renamed metrics_middleware_test.go only covers the prometheus metrics. There is also no test asserting that LoggerMiddleware's "Plugin Request Completed" output still contains the fields that were moved out of it — which is exactly why the traceID regression introduced by this PR (the explicit traceID field was removed and is no longer added anywhere in the chain) is not caught by the test suite. A small test chaining ContextualLoggerMiddleware + LoggerMiddleware and asserting the resulting log fields would lock in the intended behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` twice. If `host` is nil (e.g. an API call to POST /admin/embeddable_hosts without a host value), this raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a validation error. Guard with `self.host = self.host.to_s` or skip the substitutions when host is blank.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the EmbeddableHost before_validation callback calls sub! on a nil host, raising NoMethodError instead of allowing validation to handle the missing value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy 500 on unknown id instead of 404

`update` and `destroy` do `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` without checking the result. For a stale or invalid id (e.g. two admins, one deletes a host while the other's page still shows it), `save_host(nil)` calls `nil.host = ...` and `destroy` calls `nil.destroy`, both raising NoMethodError → 500. Additionally `save_host` dereferences `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `[:category_id]` without verifying the wrapper param exists, so any request missing the `embeddable_host` key also 500s. Raise `Discourse::NotFound` when the record doesn't exist and guard the params.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing existence check in update and destroy: an unknown ID returns nil, and subsequent calls through save_host or destroy raise NoMethodError. The additional missing-parameter concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hosts saved with a port can never match; input host not downcased for comparison

The format validation explicitly allows a port (`(:[0-9]{1,5})?`) and `before_validation` strips scheme and path but keeps the port, so an admin can save `example.com:3000`. But `record_for_host` compares `where("lower(host) = ?", uri.host)` — `uri.host` never includes the port — so that row can never match any referer and the site silently can never embed. Also the bound value isn't downcased, so a mixed-case referer host won't match `lower(host)`. Either reject/normalize ports on save or include the port (and downcase the input) in the lookup.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that record_for_host compares lower(host) against an input host that is not downcased, causing mixed-case referer hosts to fail to match. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment, despite the additional port-related concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are inserted verbatim and will never match lookups

The old `embeddable_hosts` setting supported entries with scheme and path (e.g. `http://discourse.org`, `https://example.com/1234`) — the removed specs in site_setting_spec.rb and embed_controller_spec.rb prove these worked, because the old code compared against `URI(h).host`. The migration inserts the raw setting values into the new table, but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` looks up `where("lower(host) = ?", uri.host)`, so any migrated row containing a scheme or path will never match a referer. After upgrading, previously working embedded comments silently stop working for those sites. The migration should normalize hosts the same way the model's `before_validation` does (strip scheme and path) or insert via the model.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same migration bug: raw SQL preserves schemes and paths in existing embeddable_hosts values, bypassing model normalization and causing bare-host lookups to fail. Both recommend normalizing migrated hosts to match newly created records.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents were swapped

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains all the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) that were deleted from the category file. The suite still passes only because Fabrication loads every file in the directory regardless of name, but the filenames are now actively misleading and the contents should be swapped back.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the contents of category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb were swapped, placing the fabricator definitions in the wrong files. The candidate's claim that the suite still passes does not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host values are interpolated into SQL without escaping

The INSERT interpolates the setting value directly: `VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. A value containing a single quote (legacy/malformed data in the old free-text setting) will produce invalid SQL and abort the migration. Use `ActiveRecord::Base.sanitize`/`quote` or a parameterized insert.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unescaped interpolation of host values ('#{h}') into SQL and recommend quoting or parameter binding. Although the candidate emphasizes malformed SQL rather than SQL injection, it identifies the same underlying vulnerability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting row is missing or matches no category

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. The `embed_category` setting defaulted to an empty string and is only persisted in `site_settings` if an admin actually changed it, so on most installs (and any fresh DB) the query returns zero rows, `[0]` is nil, and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and blocking the upgrade. It also crashes if the setting was set to a value that doesn't match a category name exactly. The same pattern at line 15 crashes if `uncategorized_category_id` has no row. Both lookups need nil-safe handling before indexing into the result.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked query-result indexing: when the embed_category setting is missing, the query returns no rows and accessing [0]['id'] crashes the migration. The additional cases do not change this core match.

false_positives.candidate:
embed_category is deleted even when no host rows were created

If a site used feed polling with `embed_category` set but had no `embeddable_hosts` configured (feed-only embedding, which previously worked because `TopicEmbed.import` used the global `SiteSetting.embed_category`), this migration creates zero `embeddable_hosts` rows and still deletes the `embed_category` setting. From then on `TopicEmbed.import` uses `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)` which finds nothing, so imported topics fall back to the uncategorized category — or fail validation entirely when `allow_uncategorized_topics` is false and the embedding user isn't staff. The previously configured category assignment is lost with no replacement.

Migration is not reversible despite using `change`

The migration uses `def change` but contains raw `execute` statements (data copy and `DELETE FROM site_settings`). Rolling back will raise ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration, and even a manual reverse can't restore the deleted `embeddable_hosts`/`embed_category` setting rows. This should be split into `up`/`down` with an explicit, safe down (or acknowledge irreversibility).

No foreign key or cleanup for category_id

`category_id` is `null: false` but has no foreign key, and the `EmbeddableHost` model has no `belongs_to` presence validation or dependent handling. Deleting a category leaves dangling `embeddable_hosts.category_id` values; `TopicEmbed.import` will then create topics pointing at a nonexistent category (PostCreator is given the stale id, and `ensure_topic_has_a_category` won't fix it since the id isn't nil), and the admin UI renders a missing category badge. Add a FK and/or handle category deletion.

show always renders JSON, so direct navigation/refresh to /admin/customize/embedding breaks

`show` unconditionally calls `render_serialized(...)`, which renders JSON for every format. The sibling customize pages (permalinks, colors, emojis, site texts) respond with an HTML page that boots the Ember admin app for non-XHR requests; this controller (and its missing view template) does not. Opening or refreshing `https://site/admin/customize/embedding` directly in a browser returns a raw JSON payload instead of the admin UI. Add `respond_to`/`format.html` handling plus the blank HTML view like the other admin customize controllers.

No uniqueness constraint on host

Neither the model nor the migration enforces uniqueness of `host`. The admin UI lets the same host be added multiple times with different categories, and `record_for_host` uses `.first`, so which category an embedded topic lands in becomes nondeterministic. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host` and a unique index (the migration's data copy should also dedupe).

Host validation regex rejects legitimate TLDs longer than 5 characters

The regex requires `\.[a-z]{2,5}` for the final label, so valid domains like `example.technology`, `example.international` or `example.museum` fail validation and can't be added as embedding hosts. The old free-text setting imposed no such restriction, so this is a new, undocumented limitation.

Test 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' no longer tests what it claims

`Topic#expandable_first_post?` was changed to `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?` and no longer consults embeddable hosts at all. The spec still asserts that it "is false if embeddable_host is blank", but it passes only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false — it would pass identically if a host existed, so it guards nothing about the removed condition. The example should be renamed/rewritten to reflect the new contract (or removed).

New admin endpoints have no request specs

The specs for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` (and `Admin::EmbeddingController`) only assert the class inherits from `Admin::AdminController`. All the actual behavior added in this PR — creating/updating a host, the fallback to `uncategorized_category_id` when category is blank, validation errors, unknown-id handling, destroy, and the embedding show payload — is completely untested, which is how the nil-record and nil-param crashes slip through.

Pagination support (or a higher cap) is needed on the public page, not just the admin page.

{{#unless automatic}} checks the member's automatic flag, so the remove link always renders

This template is rendered as the itemView of `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` in admin/templates/group.hbs, so its context is the member (a User), not the group. Users have no `automatic` property, so `automatic` is undefined and the `{{#unless automatic}}` guard always passes — the remove (×) link is rendered for members of automatic groups too. Clicking it triggers Admin::GroupsController#remove_member, which correctly rejects the request with a 422 (`can_not_modify_automatic`), and the client's `removeMember` action has no error handling, so the admin just gets a confusing failure. The template needs the group's flag (e.g. via the parent view/controller) instead of resolving `automatic` on the member.

limit parameter on public members endpoint is unbounded

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` accepts any value with no maximum, and this endpoint is reachable by any user who can see the group. A request with `limit=1000000` will load and serialize that many users in one request. The old code had the same flaw but only for automatic groups; it now applies to all groups. Clamp the limit (e.g. `[[limit, 200].min, 1].max`).

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count is incremented twice per failed signup because should_block? has a side effect inside validation

BlockedEmail.should_block? writes to the database (match_count += 1, last_match_at = now, save) every time it runs, and it is invoked from EmailValidator, i.e. from user validation. UsersController#create (app/controllers/users_controller.rb) calls user.valid? on line 168 and then user.save on line 172, both of which run the full validation suite, so a single signup attempt with a blocked email increments match_count by 2 and updates last_match_at twice. Any other code path that calls valid? before save does the same. The match_count/last_match_at statistics (whose purpose is explicitly described in the specs) will therefore be wrong for the primary flow they were built for. The stats update should be separated from validation (e.g. done once in the controller when a block actually rejects the signup) or made idempotent per request. The specs call should_block? directly, so they never exercise this double-run.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the email-blocking predicate mutates match statistics during a read/check operation. The candidate describes a concrete consequence—duplicate updates during validation—rather than the golden comment's concurrency and naming concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed by changing letter case

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. Nothing downcases the user's email before validation — User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] verbatim and the User model never normalizes case (unlike change_email, which uses Email.downcase). A blocked address spammer@example.com will therefore not match Spammer@example.com or SPAMMER@EXAMPLE.COM, letting a blocked user register by simply varying case. The unique index added in the migration is case-sensitive as well, so variants can coexist in the table. The lookup should compare downcased emails (and ideally the column should be normalized on write).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, which lets blocked users bypass the block by changing the capitalization of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Any server email error (e.g. 'has already been taken') marks the address as rejected and mislabels it invalid

On account-creation failure the client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email exists, and emailValidation then reports I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for that address. But errors.email is present for any email validation failure, not just blocking — most commonly the uniqueness validation (User validates :email, uniqueness: true), which produces 'has already been taken'. A user whose signup failed because the email is already registered (or who hits the ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid duplicate race after a retry) will see 'email is invalid' from then on and will be unable to re-validate that address for the rest of the session, with no hint that the real problem is a duplicate. The client should only track emails rejected specifically by the blocked-email rule (e.g. a dedicated error code from the server), not any email error.

match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write and record.save can silently fail

should_block? loads the record, does record.match_count += 1, then record.save. Two concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email both read the same match_count and one increment is lost. Additionally, the return value of record.save is ignored, so if the save fails (e.g. a validation error from a concurrent change) the statistics are silently dropped while the block decision still proceeds. Use an atomic update (e.g. update_counters or UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) for the stats bump.

Blocked-email match statistics are not recorded when another email validation already failed

The blocked check is gated on record.errors[attribute].blank?, so BlockedEmail.should_block? is never called if the email already has an error from the presence/uniqueness validators (which run before this one in User) or from the domain whitelist/blacklist check above. That means a signup attempt using a blocked email that also trips another rule — for example re-registering an email that is both blocked and already taken — leaves no trace in match_count or last_match_at, undercounting abuse attempts. If the gate exists only to avoid duplicate error messages, the stats recording should still happen and only the errors.add should be conditional.

change_email does not check the blocked list before sending the authorization email

UsersController#change_email only checks that the new email is not already in use, then creates an email token and enqueues the authorize_email message. A logged-in user can therefore request an email change to a blocked address and have the system send mail to it; the block is only (silently) enforced later if EmailToken.confirm saves the user and triggers the model validation, at which point the email change fails with no feedback to the user. The blocked check should also run in change_email so the request is rejected up front with a clear error.

float: right on .small-action button is dead because the container is now flexbox

This PR makes .small-action a flex container (@include flexbox() at the top of the rule), but the nested button still relies on `float: right` for its position. The float property has no effect on flex items, so the button rendered in small-action posts (e.g. the staff edit/action button on 'topic closed'-style posts) will no longer be pinned to the right edge of the row — it will be laid out immediately after .small-action-desc, because neither the button nor .small-action-desc has margin-left: auto or flex-grow to push it right. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button (or let .small-action-desc grow) and remove the now-inert float.

margin-left: auto used to right-align .panel does not work in the legacy box syntax the flexbox() mixin emits

.panel lost `float: right` and is now pushed to the right edge solely by `margin-left: auto` inside the flex container .contents. The flexbox() mixin applied to .contents also emits the 2009-syntax `display: -webkit-box` / `display: -moz-box` fallbacks, and the 2009 flexbox model does not support auto margins (they compute to 0). So in exactly the legacy browsers those prefixes exist for, the header icon panel will sit immediately after the title instead of at the right edge — a regression from the previous float-based layout, which worked everywhere. Either drop the 2009 display fallbacks or provide a fallback (e.g. keep a float on .panel, or use -webkit-box-pack on the container).

align-items mixin omits -moz-box-align, inconsistent with the other new flexbox mixins

The new align-items mixin emits -webkit-box-align, -ms-flex-align and modern declarations but no -moz-box-align. Its sibling mixins flexbox() and order() both include the 2009 Mozilla syntax (-moz-box, -moz-box-ordinal-group), so on Gecko versions that only implement the legacy box model, an element using these mixins becomes a -moz-box with ordering applied while the requested alignment (center in the header/small-action, baseline on category bullets) is silently ignored — the mixin half-works in exactly the engines it claims to support. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment;` for consistency (the 2009 spec accepts start/end/center/baseline/stretch).
