Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is dead code — missing '?' so AMS never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers decides whether to serialize an attribute by calling `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark), as used everywhere else in this file (`include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc.). The added method is named `include_website_name` without the `?`, so it is never invoked and `website_name` is always included in the payload — serialized as explicit null for users who have no website — instead of being omitted when `website` is blank. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (or, better, add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` as noted in the other finding, which also defines the include predicate).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but it matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the TL0/anonymous restriction that hides website

The serializer deliberately hides `website` (along with bio, location, etc.) for trust-level-0 users viewed by anonymous visitors via the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism (`include_website?` returns false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`). The new `website_name` attribute is not in the `untrusted_attributes` list, and its value is derived directly from `object.user_profile.website`, so anonymous visitors now receive `website_name` (the website's host, plus full path when it matches the instance domain) in the JSON for TL0 users even though `website` itself is withheld. This defeats the anti-spam purpose of restricting those fields. The existing spec 'doesn't serialize untrusted attributes' will not catch this because `website_name` isn't in its attribute list either. Fix by adding `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or checking `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` in its include guard) and extend the spec to cover it.

Websites Ruby's URI parser rejects (e.g. IDN/Unicode domains) disappear from the profile entirely

`URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` returns nil for any stored website that Ruby's ASCII-only URI parser cannot handle, such as non-ASCII/IDN domains. `website_name` then returns nil, and since the template renders the globe icon and link only inside `{{#if model.website_name}}`, the user's website stops being displayed on their profile at all. The previous client-side code (`website.split("/")[2]`) still displayed the domain for such URLs, so this is a regression for affected users. Consider falling back to the raw `website` string when URI parsing fails instead of returning nil.

No test for the sibling-subdomain branch of website_name

The most complex branch of `website_name` — the `elsif` that compares parent domains when website and instance hosts have equal label depth greater than 2 (e.g. show the full path for `www.example.com` on a `forum.example.com` instance, but only the host for `www.other.com`) — has no test coverage. The three added examples only exercise the equal-host case and the website-domain-is-parent case, so a regression in the parent-domain comparison would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into href attribute of posts rendered as raw HTML TopicEmbed.import appends an 'Imported from' footer built as "#{url}" with the URL inserted unescaped. The only validation is that the URL starts with http(s)://; a single quote is a valid URI character, so a feed item link or an embed URL like http://host/page'onmouseover='alert(1) breaks out of the href attribute and injects arbitrary attributes/markup into the post body. Because these posts are created with cook_method raw_html, Post#cook returns the raw string with no sanitization, and the embed view renders it via `raw post.cooked` (and the main site renders cooked verbatim), this becomes stored XSS on the forum origin for everyone who views the imported topic or embed. Escape the URL (e.g. ERB::Util.html_escape) before interpolating it into the attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import caused by interpolating an unescaped URL into generated HTML. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed items without content crash the polling job permanently

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` raises NoMethodError when an item has no content element. With simple-rss, RSS 2.0 items only expose #content when the feed includes <content:encoded>; a large number of feeds carry only <description>, and Atom entries may omit content too. One such item raises out of the each loop, aborting the whole poll (the job has retry: false), and since items are processed in feed order the same item crashes the job again on every hourly run, so no later items are ever imported. Fall back to i.description / to_s and wrap per-item processing so one bad item cannot kill the entire feed poll.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that calling i.content.scrub crashes when feed items lack content and recommend falling back to description. The candidate adds impact details and per-item error handling but describes the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer injected into a JavaScript string with only HTML escaping

The embed layout interpolates request.referer directly into a single-quoted JS string: parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>'). ERB output is HTML-escaped, which is the wrong escaping context for a JavaScript string — and in the Rails 3 boot mode this repo still supports, ERB's html_escape does not escape single quotes at all. A request to /embed/best with a Referer such as http://<embeddable-host>/';alert(1);// passes the ensure_embeddable host check (a single quote and semicolons are legal characters in a URI path) and breaks out of the JS string, executing arbitrary script inside the iframe on the forum's own origin. Use request.referer.to_json (or escape_javascript) when building the targetOrigin string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify request.referer being interpolated into JavaScript without appropriate JavaScript escaping, allowing malicious Referer content to break out of the string and execute arbitrary scripts (XSS).

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method renders remotely fetched content with zero sanitization

Post#cook now returns `raw` unchanged when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing PrettyText's sanitizer entirely. The content stored in these posts comes from remote sources: feed items via PollFeed (no filtering at all) and arbitrary pages on the embeddable host via TopicRetriever/import_remote (ruby-readability whitelists tags/attributes but still passes through href/src values such as javascript: URLs). Any script, event handler, or javascript: link in the source HTML is rendered verbatim on topic pages, in the embed iframe on the forum origin, in email digests, etc. Additionally, PostCreator now honors opts[:cook_method] for every caller (lib/post_creator.rb setup_post) — if request parameters ever flow into PostCreator opts, any user could create unsanitized raw-HTML posts, so this must be guarded against.

TopicEmbed row is created even when PostCreator rolled the post back, leaving a dangling reference

import only checks `if post.present?` before calling TopicEmbed.create!, but PostCreator#create returns the unsaved post object (with errors) when creation fails — for example when rollback_if_host_spam_detected fires, which happens for a trust-level-0 embed user importing an article that links several times to the same host (newuser_spam_host_threshold). In that case the inner Post transaction rolls back the topic and post inserts, but TopicEmbed.create! still commits a row whose topic_id/post_id point at records that no longer exist. Every subsequent /embed/best request for that URL then finds the dead topic_id and TopicView raises not-found/invalid-access, so the embed for that URL is permanently broken and the import is never retried. Check post.persisted? / post.errors.empty? instead of post.present?.

absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs Both the and rewriting treat any value starting with '/' as root-relative and rewrite it to prefix + path. Protocol-relative URLs such as //cdn.example.com/image.png (common in feeds and CMS output) also start with '/', so they are rewritten to http://host/cdn.example.com/image.png, breaking the link or image. Values starting with '//' should be left alone.

Unauthenticated endpoint enqueues unbounded outbound-fetch jobs

Any GET to /embed/best whose Referer host matches embeddable_host (a header trivially forged by non-browser clients) and that carries a previously unseen embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job, which performs an outbound HTTP fetch of that URL. The only throttle is a 60-second redis key per URL inside the job, so an attacker can enqueue unlimited jobs simply by varying the URL — exhausting sidekiq workers and directing a flood of fetches at the configured embeddable host. There should be a global or per-IP rate limit before enqueuing retrieval work.

When feed_polling_enabled? is on, perform_retrieve executes Jobs::PollFeed inline for each retrieval before falling back to direct HTTP fetch. The retrieval throttle is keyed per embed URL, so N distinct new embed URLs cause N full feed downloads/parses (and a re-import/revision pass over every feed item) inside RetrieveTopic jobs. The unused feed_key method on PollFeed suggests a per-feed throttle was intended but never wired up.

ensure_embeddable raises Discourse::InvalidAccess when request.referer is blank. Visitors using referer-stripping privacy extensions, behind referer-removing proxies, or on an HTTPS page embedding an HTTP forum (browsers omit Referer on the HTTPS→HTTP downgrade) will get an error instead of the comment embed. The check only needs to reject referers from foreign hosts; a blank referer could be treated as allowed so these users still see comments.

Imported forums lose their original chronology (topic ordering, 'x days ago' dates, digest ordering). Add a created_at option to import/import_remote and pass the thread date through.

(1) Because NOW() is not a constant default, PostgreSQL must rewrite the entire CalendarCache table to add the column, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration — on a large/busy cache table this can block writes during deployment. (2) Every pre-existing row gets updatedAt = migration time, so the new UI will display 'Last updated: <deploy time>' for all existing caches, which is misleading until each row is next written. The UI can therefore show 'Cache Status: Last updated X' and offer 'Delete cached data' for a cache that has already expired and is never served; after deletion nothing visibly changes for the user. Running it from the repo root (./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh) writes GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL to a .env file in the repository's parent directory (creating a stray file via the touch fallback) and never updates the project's actual .env. The PR adds user-facing destructive behavior with no test coverage: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds (grouping/max(updatedAt) semantics, empty credentialIds input, expired rows) and deleteCacheHandler's authorization rule (a user must not be able to delete another user's calendar cache by supplying an arbitrary credentialId). In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is an exact copy of the `start` computation — it never adds eventLength, so the upper-bound comparison `end > workingHour.endTime` only checks the slot's start. A slot that starts inside a fixed host's working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 15 minutes before the host's day ends) passes the guard and is shown as bookable, booking the host outside their availability. `end` should be derived from the slot end time (slot start + eventLength).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares two freshly created Dayjs instances by object identity, so it can never be true. The intent was evidently `.isSame()` to detect zero-length overrides (start == end, i.e. a fully blocked day). As written, blocked-day detection falls through to the other conditions, which happen to reject most slots but let a slot starting exactly at the override start pass, and the dead branch misleads anyone maintaining this logic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === compares distinct Dayjs object references rather than date values, making the comparison false. Both recommend .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
On date-override days the busy-time check is skipped entirely, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (line 133) and returns 'available' before ever evaluating the `busy.every(...)` check at line 153. Since this function is now used to validate every candidate slot against each fixed host of a round-robin event (and against loose hosts), any existing booking or calendar busy time a host has on a date-override day is ignored and the slot is offered anyway, so the host can be double-booked. A matching date override should only bypass the working-hours check; the busy/busy-calendar check must still run.

Fixed host with no working hours at all on the slot's weekday is treated as available

The new working-hours guard only rejects a slot when it finds a workingHour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday AND the slot is outside that entry's window. If the fixed host has no availability row for that weekday (e.g. they don't work weekends), `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined, the guard passes, and only busy times are checked. For a round-robin event, slots generated from another (non-fixed) host's schedule on the fixed host's day off are therefore still offered — exactly the kind of over-booking this PR is meant to prevent. A weekday with no matching working-hours entry should be treated as unavailable.

Slots inside one of several same-day override windows are rejected

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` at line 106 returns truthy as soon as ANY override on the slot's date does not contain the slot (slot ends at/before that override's start, or starts after its end). When a host has multiple override windows on the same day (e.g. 09:00–11:00 and 14:00–16:00), a slot at 10:00 is inside the first window but 'outside' the second, so find() returns the second override and the function returns false — the slot is hidden even though the host is available. The slot should be considered covered if it fits inside ANY of that day's override windows. Additionally the boundary is off by one: `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)` is strict, so a slot starting exactly at an override's end is treated as inside the override and returned as available although it lies outside every window.

The PR's headline change — applying fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours in checkIfIsAvailable for round-robin events (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts) — is only covered by manual testing steps. The single added test exercises a personal event's slot generation with a different invitee timezone. The new checkIfIsAvailable logic has several interacting branches (override match, blocked day, working-hours bounds, busy times) and contains regressions a test would catch, e.g. a fixed host with a date override plus a conflicting existing booking is currently shown as available. A round-robin scenario with a fixed host who has a date override and a busy period on that day should be added.

The invitee-local override start/end are computed as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + .minute()`. If applying `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the time across midnight — e.g. an 00:30–02:00 override for an Asia/Kolkata host viewed by a UTC-4 invitee becomes 09:30 the previous day — `.hour()/.minute()` keep only the time-of-day and the day shift is lost. Combined with the `activeOverrides` filter, which matches overrides by the organizer-local date against the invitee's day, such overrides produce slots at the wrong time on the wrong day instead of on the adjacent invitee day.

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` creates the Dayjs in the server's local timezone (no `.utc()`), while the slot side `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` is in UTC mode. The two date strings can therefore disagree for the same instant on any host not running in UTC, causing overrides to fail to match (or match the wrong day) depending on deployment timezone. Relatedly, when `organizerTimeZone` is undefined the offset silently falls back to 0, treating the override's wall-clock times as UTC.

`TimeRange.timeZone` was added as optional, but the conversion does `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` unconditionally and never falls back to the `organizerTimeZone` parameter that getSlots already receives. Any caller passing dateOverrides without a timeZone gets the server's own offset as 'organizer offset', silently converting override times as if they were UTC. The `override.start.toString()` round-trip also makes dayjs parse a non-ISO locale string instead of just passing the Date object, which is fragile and triggers dayjs's non-ISO parse warning.

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` receives the original request input rather than the filtered `uniqueGuests`. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, any attendee whose email appears in `newGuests` gets a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a brand-new 'booking confirmed' email with ics REQUEST) instead of the 'guests added' notification. So if the request redundantly included an email that was filtered out because that person is already an attendee, that existing attendee is incorrectly emailed as if they had just booked. Pass `uniqueGuests`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same misclassification: sendAddGuestsEmails checks all attendees against the raw input guests array, causing existing attendees included in that input to receive AttendeeScheduledEmail rather than AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. The candidate explicitly proposes passing the filtered uniqueGuests.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Input schema enforces neither uniqueness within guests[] nor a maximum length

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` only validates email format. The client dialog checks for duplicate emails, but the tRPC endpoint can be called directly with duplicates: the handler's filter only compares against existing booking attendees, so `createMany` inserts multiple Attendee rows with the same email for one booking, and each duplicate receives its own invitation email. The array is also unbounded, so a single request can fan out invitation emails (with event details and video link) to a very large number of arbitrary addresses. Add a uniqueness refine and a reasonable `.max(...)` to the schema.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same missing deduplication within the submitted guests array, allowing repeated emails to produce duplicate attendee rows through createMany. Its additional concern about array length does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's disableStandardEmails settings

Every other send function here (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts `eventTypeMetadata` and honors `disableStandardEmails.all.host` / `.attendee`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata and unconditionally emails the organizer, team members, and all attendees, so organizers who explicitly disabled standard emails for an event type will still trigger these 'guests added' and scheduling emails. Thread the event type metadata through and gate host/attendee emails like the other functions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor the EventType metadata's disableStandardEmails flags, causing host and attendee emails to be sent even when standard emails are disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
EventManager is built with the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

The handler constructs the EventManager via `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) })`, i.e. with the session user's credentials. But the endpoint explicitly allows callers who are not the organizer (team admins/owners and attendees). For those callers the organizer's calendar credential is not present, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` cannot update the calendar event that lives on the organizer's calendar — it will either throw (after the attendees were already persisted, and before any emails are sent, so the user sees an error toast even though the guests were added) or silently skip the update, leaving the new guests off the calendar event. Notably, the booking query already includes `user: { include: { credentials: true } }`, i.e. the organizer's credentials were fetched but never used, which strongly suggests they were the intended source. Use the booking organizer's credentials for the EventManager.

Guests are persisted before the calendar update, with no rollback or error handling

The attendee rows are created via `prisma.booking.update(...)` and only afterwards `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs outside any try/catch. If the calendar call throws (expired credential, provider API error, no matching credential), the mutation returns an error even though the guests are already in the database: no notification emails are sent (that call comes later), and a retry fails with BAD_REQUEST 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests now exist. The booking ends up with guests that nobody was notified about and no way to re-trigger the notifications. Wrap the calendar/email side effects so a failure there doesn't masquerade as a failed guest add, or perform them before/atomically with the DB write.

No validation of booking status or time before adding guests

After fetching the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. The UI only shows the action for upcoming confirmed bookings, but the tRPC endpoint itself can be called directly: an attendee or team admin can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-past booking. The handler will then create attendee records and send `AttendeeScheduledEmail` with a CONFIRMED-status ics REQUEST to arbitrary addresses for an event that is cancelled or over. Add a guard rejecting non-confirmed or past bookings.

Adding guests to seated event types bypasses seat capacity and seat records

For event types with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, attendees normally get BookingSeat/seat references and capacity is enforced. This handler inserts the new guests as plain Attendee rows via `createMany` with no seat bookkeeping and no capacity check, so a seated booking can be overbooked beyond `seatsPerTimeSlot`, and the added guests lack the seat references that seat-based flows (attendee reschedule/cancel via seatReferenceUid) rely on. Either reject seated bookings in this mutation or create proper seat records and enforce capacity.

Bookings without an owner user (dynamic bookings) crash with a 500

`prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } })` throws Prisma's NotFound error for bookings where `userId` is null (e.g. dynamic collective bookings), surfacing as an unhandled INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a clean client error. This path is reachable: for such bookings `isOrganizer` is false but an attendee passes the `isAttendee` check, then the handler 500s. Handle the missing-organizer case explicitly.

Email failures are swallowed and reported as success

`try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) } catch (err) { console.log('Error sending AddGuestsEmails') }` discards the actual error (it's not logged) and lets the mutation return success, so the user sees a 'Guests added' toast even when none of the notification/invitation emails were sent. At minimum log the error object via the standard logger, and consider surfacing the partial failure to the caller.

isInvalidEmail flag is not reset on success, so a stale error banner reappears on reopen

The dialog component stays mounted (visibility is toggled via the `open` prop), so its state persists between opens. `onSuccess` resets `multiEmailValue` but never calls `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. If a user triggers the 'Emails must be unique and valid' error, then fixes the input and submits successfully, the red error banner is still set and will be visible the next time the dialog is opened, above a fresh empty input. Reset `isInvalidEmail` in `onSuccess` (and ideally whenever the dialog closes).

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation with non-trivial authorization (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), input filtering (duplicates, blacklist), and side effects (calendar update, emails), but no tests. The permission bug alone (`isTeamAdmin && isTeamOwner` instead of an OR) and the duplicate-guest handling would have been caught by even a basic permission-matrix and input-validation test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code verification and consumption are not atomic

The authorize flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then issues a separate `prisma.user.update` to persist the remaining codes. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update commits, so a nominally single-use code can be redeemed twice within the race window. Consider consuming the code atomically (e.g., in a transaction with a re-read/optimistic check) or documenting acceptance of the risk.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: non-atomic backup-code verification and consumption allow concurrent login requests to redeem the same single-use code more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
A backup code plus any arbitrary non-empty totpCode bypasses password verification

In the credentials authorize() flow, the password check above (lines 121-129) only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`. The new backup-code branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` runs regardless of whether the password was ever verified. An attacker who knows a victim's email and one backup code (a static 10-hex-character secret, e.g. from the downloadable cal-backup-codes.txt) can log in by submitting email + backupCode + any dummy non-empty totpCode such as "000000": the presence of totpCode makes the password-verification condition false, and the backup-code branch then authenticates them and creates a session. Backup codes are intended as a second factor in addition to the password; this makes one static factor alone sufficient for account takeover. The skip exists to support the IdP totp redirect flow, but the backup-code branch should require successful password verification for CAL (password) users, or the password check should not be conditioned on totpCode being absent.

onEnable only fires from the backup-codes Close button, leaving stale state on other dismiss paths

Before this change, `onEnable()` (which makes the parent settings page refresh and show the 2FA switch as enabled) ran immediately when /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable returned 200. It is now replaced with `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and only called from the "Close" button on the backup-codes screen. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way — the dialog's X button, Escape key, or overlay click, all routed through `onOpenChange` — `onEnable()` never runs, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled even though it is now on (until a manual refetch), and `resetState()` also doesn't run, so reopening the modal lands on the stale backup-codes screen displaying the old codes. The parent notification/state reset should happen on any close of the final step, not just the Close button.

Backup codes cannot be used by Google/SAML users in the IdP two-factor challenge

When a Google/SAML user with 2FA signs in, they are redirected to /auth/login?totp=<jwt>, which renders the TOTP input with `ExternalTotpFooter` — only a Cancel button, no "Lost access" option — so there is no way in the UI to enter a backup code. A backup-code-only request is also rejected server-side: in next-auth-options.ts the guards `user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode` (lines 113-121) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled / IncorrectEmailPassword before the new backup-code branch is reached. Consequence: identity-provider users who lose their authenticator remain locked out despite having valid backup codes; the recovery feature only works for CAL password accounts.

Consumed backup codes are nulled in place instead of removed

After a successful backup-code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is persisted rather than splicing the used code out of the array. The stored JSON keeps accumulating null placeholders, `user.backupCodes` stays truthy forever, and once all 10 codes have been used the user gets `IncorrectBackupCode` instead of an indication that their codes are exhausted (`MissingBackupCodes` only fires when codes were never generated). Splice the redeemed code out and treat an empty array the same as having no backup codes.

missing_backup_codes message instructs users to do something impossible

The new string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown on the login page when a user with 2FA enabled but no backup codes uses the "Lost access" flow — i.e., users who enabled 2FA before this feature existed and are now locked out of their authenticator. There is no settings UI to (re)generate backup codes for an account that already has 2FA enabled (codes are only created during initial setup), and a locked-out user cannot reach settings anyway. The recovery instruction cannot be followed and will generate support tickets.

First 2FA e2e test not updated for the new backup-code screen; its assertion is admittedly broken

In "should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA", after the OTP is accepted the modal now displays the backup-codes screen, but the test never interacts with it or closes it (unlike the second test, which was updated). The subsequent check on the switch state is annotated with a newly added FIXME stating it passes even when the switch is not checked, and since `onEnable` now only fires from the backup-codes Close button, the enabled state is never confirmed. This test would stay green even if enabling 2FA regressed. It should close the backup-code screen and assert on `data-state="checked"` like the second test does.

No test covers logging in with a backup code or its one-time-use guarantee

The security-critical behavior introduced by this PR — authenticating with a backup code, rejecting an invalid code, and consuming a code so it cannot be reused — has no automated coverage. The added test code only checks the download filename and the copy toast, and a TODO acknowledges the missing tests. A regression making backup codes reusable, unconsumed, or rejected would ship undetected.

navigator.clipboard used without an availability check

The Copy button calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` directly. The Clipboard API is only exposed in secure contexts; on self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP, `navigator.clipboard` is undefined, so clicking Copy throws a TypeError and the user gets no feedback at all (the success toast is never reached). Feature-detect `navigator.clipboard` and fall back to a hidden-textarea copy, or show an error toast.

Google Meet fallback crashes when booking has no destination calendar

In `create()`, the code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then evaluates `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` when `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. When the event has no destination calendar (`null` from handleNewBooking, or `[]` from confirm/payment flows), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and reading `.integration` throws a TypeError. This is exactly the scenario this branch exists for ("Fallback to Cal Video if Google Meet is selected w/o a Google Cal"), so any booking with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar now crashes instead of falling back to Daily. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`); this needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

Although it discusses create() rather than explicitly covering both createEvent() and updateEvent(), the cause and failure scenario match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

That `.find` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it compares each calendar's `externalId` against `null`/`""` and can never match — `selectedCalendar` is always `undefined` in that case, and `calendar.events.update` is then called with `calendarId: undefined`, which throws and leaves the Google event un-updated (caught upstream as success=false, so the booking is rescheduled in cal.com but the calendar event keeps the old time). The previous code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. This matters more now because other changes in this PR create references with `externalCalendarId: null` (see EventManager updateLocation and the no-credentialId create branch). This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED condition for org slug is inverted

This PR (which is about destination calendars) changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the condition. Previously, when team billing was disabled (e.g. self-hosted), the org got its `slug` immediately, and when billing was enabled only `requestedSlug` was stored so the real slug could be set after payment. After this change, billing-enabled installs set `slug` before payment (bypassing the paid flow) and billing-disabled installs never set a slug at all, leaving the organization without a usable URL. false_positives.candidate:
Video booking references lose credentialId, breaking meeting deletion on cancel

In `create()`'s `referencesToCreate`, the credentialId is now `isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously it was `isCalendarType ? evt.destinationCalendar?.credentialId : result.credentialId`, i.e. video results kept `result.credentialId` from `createMeeting`. With this change, every newly created video BookingReference is stored with `credentialId: null`. `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set (it looks up the credential by id to call `deleteMeeting`), so cancelling bookings created after this change will leave orphaned Zoom/Daily/etc. meetings that are never deleted. There is no reason to special-case calendar types here; use `result.credentialId` for all results.

updateLocation references are created without credentialId/externalCalendarId

`updateLocation()` now builds references with `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined`, but the calendar-update results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned EventResult never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Both fields are therefore always `undefined`, and `editLocation.handler` persists these references on the booking (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`). The old code fell back to `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` / `?.credentialId`. Consequence: bookings that go through "edit location" accumulate calendar references with no credential/calendar linkage, so later updates/deletes can't find the right credential and fall into legacy paths (including the broken Google `updateEvent` fallback).

Office365 createEvent always targets the main host's calendar, even when creating for another host

`createEvent` now takes the first entry of `event.destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`) and posts to `/me/calendars/{mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId}/events`. For collective events, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` calls `createEvent` once per host with that host's credential, but the full event (with all destination calendars, main host first) is passed each time. So when creating the event for a non-organizer host's Office365 account, it tries to write to the main host's calendar id using the team member's token, which fails (404/403) — the team member never gets the event. `CalendarManager.createEvent` already receives the per-destination `externalId` but doesn't forward it to `calendar.createEvent`; the credentialId-based lookup used in the Google service (or forwarding externalId) is needed here too.

Lark createEvent uses the first destination calendar regardless of which host's credential is used

Same class of bug as the Office365 service: `createEvent` derives `calendarId` from `event.destinationCalendar[0]` (the main host's calendar). For collective bookings, EventManager invokes `createEvent` separately for each host's credential, but Lark will always attempt `POST /calendar/v4/calendars/{mainHostCalendarId}/events/create_event` with the team member's token, which the member has no access to — so non-organizer hosts never get Lark calendar events. The service should select the destination calendar matching the credential being used (as the Google service now does with the credentialId parameter).

CalDAV createEvent silently reports success without creating anything for other hosts

The CalDAV base service filters `calendars` to `c.externalId === mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` where `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. When EventManager creates the event for a non-organizer host's CalDAV credential (collective events), that host's account does not contain the main host's calendar URL, so the filtered list is empty, `Promise.all([])` resolves to `[]`, `responses.some(r => !r.ok)` is false, and the method returns a successful result with a uid — but no event was created anywhere. This is a silent data-integrity failure: the booking reference is stored, but the team member's calendar has no event. It should match the destination calendar for the credential in use, like Google's credentialId lookup.

Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer and event type have none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective-team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining means that when the base value is `null`, the push is silently skipped: for a collective event where the organizer has no connected destination calendar but team members do, none of the team members' calendars receive events (and the booking's destinationCalendar is not connected either). The array should be initialized to `[]` (or the team calendars assigned directly) so collective hosts still get their events.

Dynamic user query no longer selects organization

The `loadUsers` refactor rewrote the dynamic-group user lookup and dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select (it was explicitly selected before, together with `metadata`). Any downstream code for dynamic collective bookings that reads `user.organization.slug` (e.g. org-subdomain/booker-url handling) will now get `undefined` and potentially throw. This removal is unrelated to the destination-calendar change and looks accidental; it should be restored.

Recurring-event deletion block now runs once per calendar reference

The recurring-cancellation branch (mapping over all of the organizer's calendar credentials × all updated recurring bookings and deleting each) lives inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the collective multi-host case this PR introduces, typically one per host), the entire recurring deletion pass executes once per reference, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for the same events. Google tolerates this via 404/410 handling, but other providers may log errors and it doubles the external API traffic. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop. (Separately, that branch still only deletes the first calendar reference per updated booking, so team-member calendar events for recurring collective bookings remain stale.)

Hangout-link patch call uses possibly-undefined calendarId

In `createEvent`, the insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (that writes the description with the hangout link) passes the raw `selectedCalendar`, which is `undefined` whenever no destination calendar matches the credentialId. The google client will throw a missing-parameter error for that patch, so the hangout link is never written into the event description in that case. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always defined (defaulted to "primary").

Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging bookings on reschedule

When `newBookingId` is set (reschedule/merge path), the code deletes the old booking's calendar event via `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`. Bookings can now have multiple calendar references (one per collective host), so only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep a stale event at the old time. This should iterate over all calendar references of the old booking.

Webhook payload sends destinationCalendar as null in some flows and [] in others

The updated e2e expectations now encode that BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED payloads contain `destinationCalendar: null` while BOOKING_REJECTED contains `destinationCalendar: []` — because handleNewBooking emits `null` when there is no destination calendar while confirm.handler emits `[]`. This is an inconsistent contract for the same field across webhook triggers, and the field's shape also changed from a single object to an array, which is a breaking change for existing webhook consumers despite the PR being labelled non-breaking. Consider normalizing (always array, or always null-when-empty) across all emitters.

No automated tests cover the new multi-destination calendar logic

The PR rewrites `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` and the create/update/delete paths of four calendar providers for the collective multi-host scenario, but the author explicitly checked "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". The only test change is a webhook payload expectation. Regressions introduced here (e.g. the Google Meet fallback TypeError, non-Google providers writing to the main host's calendar, video references losing credentialId) would be caught by even a minimal unit test around `EventManager.create` with multiple destination calendars.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
App API dispatcher still reads the appStore barrel synchronously, breaking all app OAuth callbacks and app webhooks

This PR changes every value of the default export of `@calcom/app-store` from the app's module namespace to a Promise of that namespace. The catch-all API route `apps/web/pages/api/integrations/[...args].ts`, which dispatches every app's API endpoints (`/api/integrations/{app}/add`, `/callback`, `/webhook`, etc. — e.g. the Google Calendar OAuth callback and the Stripe payment webhooks) looks the app up synchronously as `const app = appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` and then checks `"api" in app` before calling `app.api[endpoint](req, res)`. It is not among the updated files, so after this change `app` is a Promise, the `in` check is false, and the route falls through to its error/404 path for every app. Consequence: connecting/disconnecting any integration and all payment webhooks stop working. The lookup must become `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]`. It is also worth grepping the whole repo for any other remaining `appStore[...]` / `getCalendar(` consumers, since the barrel's contract changed from synchronous module to Promise and only the call sites in this PR were migrated.

The dynamic imports still execute eagerly — importing the barrel immediately loads all 28 app chunks

Each registry entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`, so every `import()` expression is invoked at the moment `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. Only the *awaiting* became lazy, not the *loading*: the first import of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers fetching and evaluating all 28 app modules, so the startup/module-load cost this PR is presumably trying to reduce is essentially unchanged (only code-splitting/parallel async evaluation is gained). If the intent is to load an app only when it is actually used, the values need to be thunks (`() => import("./applecalendar")`) or a lazy getter/Proxy, with call sites adjusted accordingly. A side effect of creating all 28 promises up front is that a chunk-load failure in an app that is never used still produces an unhandled promise rejection (most entries are never awaited), which crashes Node under the default unhandled-rejections behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
error-invalid-multivalued-size switched to Java MessageFormat choice syntax that the i18next-based admin console cannot render

This key was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The keycloak.v2 admin console formats these messages client-side with react-i18next, whose interpolation syntax is `{{0}}` (which is why the previous value used it) and which has no support for Java's `{2,choice,...}` clause. When this error is displayed for a multivalued attribute validation failure, the console will show the raw pattern text instead of substituting the attribute name and bounds. The server-side bundles (themes/.../admin and themes/.../login messages_en.properties) can use this syntax because they are formatted with java.text.MessageFormat, but the React console bundles must keep `{{0}}`-style placeholders.

error-invalid-multivalued-size switched to Java MessageFormat choice syntax that the i18next-based account console cannot render

This key was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The keycloak.v3 account console renders these messages with i18next (`{{0}}` interpolation, as used by the previous version of this key), and vanilla i18next cannot evaluate a Java `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` expression — the choice clause will be displayed literally and the `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` placeholders won't follow this file's interpolation convention. Users hitting this validation error will see the raw format string instead of a readable message.

Anchor validation requires identical anchors in identical order and stops at the first mismatch

In `santizeAnchors` the n-th anchor found in the translation is compared with the n-th anchor found in the English source using sequential `find()` calls. A translation that contains exactly the same anchors as the source but in a different order — legitimate when grammar or right-to-left mirroring reorders links in a sentence — is reported as "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string" and fails the build. Additionally the `break` after the first mismatch means any further anchors in the same value are never validated. Comparing against the multiset/list of English anchors (membership instead of positional matching) would avoid these false positives.

verifySafeHtml throws bare RuntimeException when a properties file can't be read, bypassing the MojoExecutionException contract

`verify()` declares `MojoExecutionException` and converts IO failures of the primary file read into it, but the new `verifySafeHtml()` opens the target file and the derived English file again and throws plain `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` on failure (also at line 70). This happens, for example, when a community locale file has no English counterpart under `resources/`, so adding a new translation can crash the Maven plugin with an internal-error stack trace instead of a clean, file-named plugin error or a regular verification message. These exceptions should be wrapped in `MojoExecutionException` (or reported as verification messages) for consistent error reporting.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed, replayable forever, and cannot be removed

With this PR a recovery-code credential can now live in an external user storage, but the 'single use' semantics of recovery codes are lost on that path. For locally stored codes, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid() marks the used code as consumed so it cannot be replayed and the next login asks for the next unused code. For a federated credential, validation is delegated to the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() (a read-only boolean check, see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) and nothing ever marks a code as used, so the credential reconstructed from the storage always shows all 12 codes as unused. Consequences: (1) every recovery code of a storage-backed user stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed by anyone who observed it once; (2) the login form always asks for code #1, because RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() on an all-unused credential, so code rotation never happens; (3) the cleanup here at lines 85-88 calls credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's own store — the CredentialInputUpdater SPI has no remove-by-id operation for external storages — so even an exhausted federated credential would silently never be deleted (likewise, admin delete/disable of such a credential is a no-op in the sample provider). The new test BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.enterRecoveryCodes actually bakes in the always-code-#0 behavior rather than detecting it. Before merging, used-code state should be pushed back to the storage (e.g., via CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation explicitly documented and tested.

Raw recovery codes are sent to and persisted in user storage as plaintext JSON

In CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, when the credential is delegated to a user storage, the raw, unhashed recovery codes are serialized (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes) at line 119) and passed to CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential as the UserCredentialModel challenge response, so the external store persists all 12 valid codes in plaintext JSON. When the same credential is created locally (line 129), only SHA-512 hashes are stored, because RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes each code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode. Consequence: for storage-backed users, anyone with read access to the external store (database, backups, logs) immediately obtains working recovery codes that bypass the second factor entirely — a weaker protection level than Keycloak's own store provides for the identical data. The sample provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage mirrors this by storing the plaintext JSON and comparing the presented code in cleartext. The hashed credential data (credentialModel.getCredentialData()) could be sent to the storage instead, with validators hashing the presented code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode before comparing, so both storage paths keep only hashes.

User label and original generation timestamp are dropped when recovery codes go to user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential builds the UserCredentialModel sent to the user storage with only the JSON array of codes; the generatedUserLabel (collected from the setup form and applied to the locally created credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues) and the generatedAt timestamp are never transmitted. The sample storage (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential, recovery-codes branch) therefore stores createdDate = write time and userLabel = null. Consequence: the same setup flow produces different credential metadata depending on where the credential lands — the label the user assigned is silently lost for storage-backed users and createdDate no longer reflects when the codes were generated, which shows up incorrectly in the account console and breaks parity between the two paths. The label and generation time should be included in the payload sent to CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 silently repurposed from 'recreate upgrade required' to 'feature disabled'

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3, and 4 now means FEATURE_DISABLED. The update-compatibility tool is explicitly documented as 'fully scriptable' and its exit codes are the supported contract for CI/CD pipelines. Any automation written against the previous preview that branches on exit code 4 to decide that a recreate upgrade is required will now misinterpret that case: a 'recreate required' result returns 3 (which such a script would treat as an unknown error), and a 'feature disabled' result returns 4 (which it would treat as 'recreate required', potentially triggering an unnecessary full shutdown and downtime). The docs table is updated in this PR, but existing scripts get no warning. If this renumbering is intentional, it should at least be called out in the release notes/upgrading guide so adopters of the preview can update their pipelines.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the exit code renumbering as a breaking change for scripts. It explicitly recommends calling it out in the release notes/upgrading guide so users can migrate, which is the golden comment's concern.

The check subcommand's feature-disabled branch (UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run) has no coverage, and neither test asserts the exit code, even though the documentation added in this PR advertises exit code 4 ('The feature rolling-updates is disabled') as part of the scripting contract. A regression where picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) returns the wrong code (e.g., 0 or 1) would silently break the automation contract this PR documents. The feature is only required when spec.update.strategy is configured on the Keycloak CR. As written, users who never set an update strategy will be told they must enable a preview feature to keep the Operator from failing, which is not true. Reword to scope the requirement, e.g. 'When spec.update.strategy is configured, the preview feature rolling-updates must be enabled; otherwise the Operator will fail to process the update.'

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down on the first rebalance; all later messages are silently dropped but their offsets committed

FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is passed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_with_partitions. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which calls shutdown() on each internal queue.Queue. After the first rebalance the factory hands the already-shut-down pool to the new strategy: FixedQueuePool.submit's work_queue.put(...) raises queue.ShutDown, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and then marks the message's offset as completed, so the background commit thread commits offsets for messages that were never processed. Net effect: after any rebalance (deploy, scaling, partition movement) the consumer silently drops every subsequent message while advancing committed offsets — silent data loss plus one exception log per message — until the process is restarted. The shared OffsetTracker also retains state for revoked partitions, so the new commit thread will attempt to commit offsets for partitions this consumer no longer owns. The pool should be created per create_with_partitions call (or close() should not shut down a factory-owned pool), and a rebalance test is missing.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit when processing lags

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so put() never blocks and queued work is unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit is called synchronously from the StreamProcessor poll loop, meaning that when processing is slower than intake — the exact scenario this PR is designed to mitigate — messages are continuously pulled from Kafka and accumulated in memory, growing consumer RSS until OOM and inflating consumer lag. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring advertises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false with unbounded queues. Use bounded queues (a blocking put naturally throttles the poll loop) or pause consumption when queue depth exceeds a threshold.

A single permanent offset gap wedges all future commits for a partition and the per-second scan grows unboundedly

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets only advances the committable offset through a strictly contiguous integer range (for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)). Any permanent gap in a partition's offsets blocks commits for that partition forever: Kafka topics written by transactional producers contain control-record batches that consume offsets without ever being delivered to the consumer, and compacted topics have gaps by design. Once wedged, the committed offset never advances, so every restart replays the entire post-gap backlog, and the commit loop re-scans range(start, max_offset + 1) every second, growing by one iteration per new message and burning ever-increasing CPU in the commit thread. The new tests (test_offset_gaps_block_commits) enshrine gap-blocking as intended, but it does not match Kafka offset semantics; iterating over sorted(all_offsets) and blocking only on seen-but-still-outstanding offsets would handle gaps without losing safety for submitted-but-unfinished work.

Shutdown stops the commit thread before workers finish; final completed offsets are never committed and queued work is dropped

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the background commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any offsets that workers complete after the commit thread exits (in-flight items at shutdown — common here since this mode targets slow items) are never committed and will be reprocessed on restart. Additionally, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so each worker exits after finishing only its current item and all remaining queued items are discarded rather than drained, despite the 'gracefully shutdown' docstring (their offsets stay uncommitted, so this is reprocessing rather than loss, but it discards the backlog on every deploy/rebalance). Finally, join(timeout) ignores its timeout argument and just calls close() again, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() joins each of the N workers with its own 5s timeout, so strategy shutdown can take up to ~5*N seconds (default N=20 → ~100s) regardless of the join_timeout the StreamProcessor requested.

test_stats_reporting races with live worker threads and can flake on total_items > 0

In TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 work items and then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 while three real worker threads (started in setUp) are actively draining the queues. If the main thread is preempted during the submit loop (e.g., on a loaded CI machine), the workers can process all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making total_items 0 and failing the assertion intermittently. The test should block processing (e.g., with a threading.Event the result processor waits on) before asserting a nonzero queue depth.

For such discover queries on fully allowlisted projects, `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (sum of sample_weight) even though the result set contains non-error events that have no sample_weight, so the returned counts are NULL or undercounted relative to the real totals. The check should parse the query or at minimum reject matches that are negated or inside quotes.

upsampled_count drops rows with NULL sample_weight, silently undercounting

The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` ignores NULLs, so any error row whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes nothing at all — not even 1. That covers errors ingested before a project was added to the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (still inside retention) and errors stored without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context — the PR's own test-factory change only sets `sample_rate` when that context is present, demonstrating such rows exist. The result is that upsampled counts for allowlisted projects can be lower than the true event count, with no indication to the user. Wrapping the column, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`, would make unsampled rows count as 1.

Cache-invalidation helper is never called, so allowlist changes are stale for up to 60s with no escape hatch

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is added with a docstring saying it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in this PR or elsewhere calls it — there is no hook on the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option. As shipped, edits to the allowlist take up to the 60-second cache TTL to take effect and there is no way to force invalidation, while the dead function implies an invalidation path that does not exist. Either wire it into the option-change path or remove it.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

In Service.Check, the permission-denial cache is consulted first and short-circuits the request, before the permission cache is checked for an allow. A denial entry is written only after a fresh DB lookup denies, but it then lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). Meanwhile, any DB re-query for the same user+action (triggered by a check on a different resource, or by cache expiry) rewrites the entire permCache scope map with fresh permissions, because getUserPermissions always calls permCache.Set after fetching. Concrete sequence: t0 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) denies and caches a denial for dash1; t1 the user is granted access to dash1 and dash2; t2 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash2) misses the cached scope map, re-queries the DB, allows, and repopulates permCache with permissions that now include dash1; t3 Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) hits the stale denial entry and returns Allowed=false even though the server's own permission cache (and the DB) would allow it. The user stays denied for that resource until the denial entry expires. This partially undermines the PR's stated goal (a single check that races the permission write poisons the resource for 30s). Checking the permission cache for an allow before consulting the denial cache would preserve the fast-deny path while preventing stale denials from overriding fresher allow data the server already holds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"] for integrations that lack sender metadata

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the new check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration row has `sender` in its metadata. That is not true: `build_integration` only stores `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is set, and integrations created through the normal in-Sentry pipeline never have it (the PR's own test_basic_flow asserts the final metadata contains only access_token/expires_at/icon/domain_name/account_type). Only integrations created by the installation webhook carry `sender`. This code path is reachable whenever an ACTIVE Integration exists with no OrganizationIntegration — e.g. the owning organization was deleted, orphaning the Integration row — and someone then installs the same GitHub App installation into another Sentry organization. In that case `integration.metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended github-integration-failed.html page, with no way to complete the install. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and define explicit fail-open/fail-closed behavior for integrations without sender metadata.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is accessed without checking that the 'sender' key exists, which raises a KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Network/API failures during token exchange and /user fetch are unhandled and produce 500s

OAuthLoginView.dispatch performs two outbound HTTP calls that can raise: `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` (line 423) is outside the try/except (the try only covers safe_urlread/parsing), and `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) has no exception handling at all. A DNS/connection failure or timeout to github.com, or a non-JSON error body from the api.github.com/user call (resp.json() raises), will propagate out of the pipeline and return a 500 to the user, instead of the graceful github-integration-failed.html error page this PR introduces for every other verification failure. These calls should be wrapped and converted into the same error response (ideally with logging), since transient GitHub/network errors in a user-facing auth pipeline are expected.

Fresh-install path performs no verification that the OAuth user controls the installation

When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` and `build_integration` fetches `/app/installations/{installation_id}` using the GitHub App JWT — which can read ANY installation of the Sentry GitHub App. GitHub App installation IDs are sequential/enumerable, and the OAuth step only proves the attacker's own GitHub identity; on this path it is never compared to anything about the installation. So if the Integration row does not exist yet — the installation.created webhook is delayed, permanently failed to deliver, or webhooks aren't configured/reachable (self-hosted) — anyone who knows or guesses a victim's installation_id can attach the victim's GitHub organization installation to their own Sentry organization, exposing its repositories, commits, CODEOWNERS and source-linking data. The sender check added here only helps once the webhook-created row exists. Consider additionally verifying on the fresh path that the authenticated GitHub user belongs to / admins the installation's account (e.g. via the installation account and an org-membership check), rather than skipping verification entirely.

GitHub integration install now hard-requires the github-login OAuth app to be configured

OAuthLoginView pulls `client_id`/`client_secret` from GitHubIdentityProvider (the github-login identity OAuth app, e.g. the `github-login.client-id`/`github-login.client-secret` options), which is a separate configuration from the GitHub App (github-app.* options) that the integration previously needed. On deployments that have the GitHub App configured but never set up the github-login identity provider (a plausible self-hosted configuration), these values are None/empty: the pipeline will redirect to GitHub's authorize URL with an invalid client_id (GitHub shows an error) or the token exchange will fail, making the GitHub integration uninstallable where it previously worked. There is no feature flag, fallback, or documentation noting this new requirement. Consider gating the new step on the OAuth app being configured, or explicitly failing with a clear operator-facing error/docs update.

No positive-path test for the sender-match flow, and no test for integrations missing sender metadata

The new tests only cover the negative case (test_github_user_mismatch: webhook-created Integration whose sender does not match the OAuth user). There is no test that exercises the main protected flow end-to-end: installation webhook creates the Integration with a sender, the same GitHub user completes the OAuth step, the sender check passes, and the installation links successfully (the direct-from-GitHub install path). A regression that breaks legitimate installs from GitHub would not be caught. There is also no test with a pre-existing ACTIVE Integration whose metadata lacks `sender`, which would have exposed the KeyError in `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` reported separately.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update is computed against the org-aware wrapped model, so updates made while the org is disabled can leave stale login entries

In update(), the current state of the IDP is loaded via getById(model.getInternalId()), which returns the organization-aware wrapper produced by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled, deleted, or the OrganizationProvider is unavailable. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on this wrapped original: while the org is disabled, test(original) is always false, so the first early-return (!test(original) && !test(updated)) fires for any update that also makes the updated model fail the predicate — e.g. an admin sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or disables the raw IDP on a broker belonging to a disabled org. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)

GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem in GetWebAssets: the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired, which makes the double-checked locking incomplete.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
