Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)

GetWebAssets first reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock (lines 41-43), then acquires the write lock at line 48 and unconditionally reloads the manifest from disk (readWebAssetsFromFile at line 60) and republishes the cache. Because there is no second check after the write lock is acquired, any requests that arrive concurrently before the cache is first populated will each perform the full manifest load sequentially and overwrite each other's cache entry. Besides duplicated disk I/O, a transient read error in a later goroutine can replace an already-populated good cache entry with nil and return an error to its caller even though a valid cached value existed. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after taking the write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment's main point is that the fetch result is assigned to the cache unconditionally, so a failed fetch writes nil over a valid cache entry. The candidate's main point is the missing double-check after taking the write lock. It does also say that a transient read error can replace a good cache entry with nil, which is the same failure the golden comment describes. Its proposed fix is the double-check rather than skipping the assignment on error, but it still identifies the cache being overwritten with nil on error. That makes it a partial but meaningful match.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held across manifest file I/O, serializing all GetWebAssets callers

The deferred Unlock at line 49 keeps entryPointAssetsCacheMu held while readWebAssetsFromFile (line 60) opens, reads, and parses assets-manifest.json from disk. While the write lock is held, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks — including callers that would otherwise be served by the read-locked fast path, since RLock cannot proceed while the write lock is held. In dev mode (setting.Dev) the fast path is skipped by design, so every index page load now serializes on this disk I/O, and on a slow filesystem all such requests stall behind a single global mutex. Loading and parsing the manifest outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid this.

The PR adds a mutex to guard the package-level entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. A data-race fix without a test that exercises concurrent access can silently regress. A test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines against a temporary assets-manifest.json (with cfg.Env set to a non-dev value so the cache path is exercised) and is run with the race detector enabled (`go test -race`) would have caught the original race and would verify the fix going forward.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs only guards SQLite's parameter limit; oversized batch sizes fail on Postgres/MySQL

deleteByIDs builds DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with one bind parameter per ID and only switches away from parameters for SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999. On other databases the batch size is configurable and unvalidated: if it is set above the driver's bind-parameter cap (65535 for Postgres, and MySQL prepared statements have a similar 65535 placeholder limit), every cleanup batch will fail with a parameter-count error, so cleanup never makes progress. The previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter list at all, so this is a regression for large configured batch sizes. Consider chunking the ID slice to a safe per-statement size (e.g. 1000) for all dialects.

In the SQLite branch of deleteByIDs the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n^2) work. With the batch size this path is designed for (e.g. 32767 IDs, as exercised by the new test), that is on the order of gigabytes of byte copying per batch, repeated on every cleanup cycle while a backlog exists. Using a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-formatted values) would make it linear.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the asynchronous legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is created with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), deriving from the incoming request context. In the Kubernetes API server the request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write completes. The detached goroutine therefore almost always executes with an already-canceled context and the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' — in mode 3 the legacy copy (the stated 'safe measure') is silently skipped, with only a metric recording the failure. The goroutine should first detach values from the request lifecycle, e.g. ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the 10s timeout.

Update passes raw UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy, so UpdatedObject runs twice and the two stores can diverge

Update now hands the raw rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update, meaning objInfo.UpdatedObject() is executed independently by each store against its own old object. The previous implementation resolved the object once (Storage.Get + UpdatedObject) and wrapped the result in updateWrapper so both stores persisted the identical object. With the new code, create-on-update paths that generate names/UIDs produce different objects in legacy vs unified storage, and any mutating logic inside UpdatedObject runs twice, so the two stores can silently hold divergent objects — exactly what dual write is meant to prevent. The object should be materialized once and the frozen result passed to the legacy update via updateWrapper, as before.

Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy-only objects can never be deleted

Delete now returns immediately on any error from unified storage, including NotFound. The previous implementation special-cased apierrors.IsNotFound and still issued the legacy delete. With the new early return, an object that exists only in legacy storage (created before unified storage was enabled, or left behind by a failed dual write) can never be deleted in mode 3: callers receive NotFound and the stale legacy row remains forever.

Mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy API state synchronously, racing the async legacy write

The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' subtest (line 132) and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtest (line 191) run the full doPlaylistTests suite, which checks legacy API state immediately after k8s writes — e.g. listing /api/playlists right after k8s Create and getFromBothAPIs right after k8s Update. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous (a goroutine with up to a 10s window), so these assertions race it and will flake: the legacy endpoint can still 404 or return the pre-update title. The mode-3 runs need eventually/polling-style assertions for legacy-side reads, or the legacy-side checks should be skipped for mode 3.

Storage create/update failures are recorded in the legacy-duration metric

When the unified-storage Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a legacy failure that never happened (legacy is never called on this path) into the legacy duration metric, with the storage start time, and never recording the actual storage failure. The same bug exists in Update at line 129. Both should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics that distinguish legacy vs unified errors.

The previous code rendered <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../>, and the 'datasource' and 'default' branches still pass key={key}, but the 'grafana' branch now renders <GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={...} ... /> with no key prop. Pass key={key} as before.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered in a list without a key prop, which can cause reconciliation problems when items are reordered.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. With rulerRule undefined the drawer is never rendered, so the silence action silently does nothing. skipToken path returns enabled abilities, granting Duplicate on cloud rules based on Grafana permissions

With rule undefined, useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable returns loading:false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported, isPluginProvided/isProvisioned are false, and the abilities are computed with getRulesPermissions('grafana'): Duplicate becomes [true, ctx.hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]. As a result a user who has the Grafana-managed rule create permission but NOT AlertingRuleExternalWrite will now see the Duplicate menu item on cloud rules (previously only the ruler-based ability, which checks the external-write permission for that data source, was used). The skipToken/undefined-rule path should yield all-disabled abilities instead of permission-evaluated ones.

Before this change, useAllAlertRuleAbilities (still used via useAlertRuleAbility by CombinedRule consumers such as the existing RulesTable) computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made Update/Delete/Pause unsupported for federated (cross-tenant) Mimir/GEM rule groups. The hook now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only receives a RulerRuleDTO and hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. Consequently, for rules in federated groups the Edit/Delete/Pause abilities become 'supported' again and the corresponding buttons/menu items reappear; attempting the operation will fail against the ruler or, worse, modify a group the UI intentionally treated as immutable. The federated check needs to be preserved somewhere in the new delegation chain.

In useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, ModifyExport is computed as [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed] where isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The ruler-based equivalent uses isGrafanaManagedAlertRule = rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule), which matches both Grafana alerting AND recording rules, so recording rules currently expose the 'Export / With modifications' menu item (the modify-export flow supports recording rules). In the new ruler-less list view the rulerRule is absent, so canExport relies solely on the prom-based ability and recording rules lose the Export menu entry. The same narrowing applies to Pause/Restore (Grafana recording rules are pausable, but the prom-based ability requires an alerting rule), which will bite once the pause menu item is wired to prom rules.

The previous GrafanaRuleListItem (in the deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx) built the rule href as createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo }) using createReturnTo(), so navigating back from the rule detail view returned the user to the originating (possibly filtered) rule list. The new component builds `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` with no returnTo, so the detail view's back navigation falls back to the default alert list and loses the user's list context/filters. Re-add the returnTo parameter.

Stale comment about preloading ruler rules after ruler prefetch was removed

The diff removes the alertRuleApi prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...) dispatch but leaves the comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX. Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded' and the variable name cacheAndRulerPreload. The comment now describes behavior that no longer exists and is misleading about what the remaining upsertQueryData does; update the comment and rename the variable.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting defeats the $__range no-splitting guard

runSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (line 299) before partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query)) runs on the next line. applyTemplateVariables substitutes the built-in range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from scopedVars, and dashboard/Explore requests always carry those scoped vars. querySupportsSplitting() decides a query must not be split by calling isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr), which searches for the literal text '$__range' — but by the time it runs, that text has already been replaced (e.g. count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) has become count_over_time({a="b"}[30d])). Consequence: queries using $__range are now time-split instead of being routed to nonSplittingQueries and executed once over the full range, which is exactly what the comment above the check says must not happen. Besides contradicting the documented intent, this is a real cost/correctness regression for large ranges: with a 30-day dashboard, each 1-day chunk evaluates count_over_time(...[30d]), re-scanning ~30 days of data per chunk (~30x the scanned volume of the previous single request). The existing unit tests do not catch this because the test requests carry no scopedVars, so $__range survives interpolation in tests but not in production. The isQueryWithRangeVariable check should run on the raw, pre-interpolation expr — or, if splitting such queries is now intentional, the dead check and its misleading comment should be removed.

Queries are now interpolated two to three times (runShardSplitQuery / runSplitQuery / runQuery)

Interpolation is now applied repeatedly to the same targets. LokiDatasource.runQuery — which the splitting code calls for every sub-request (runSplitGroupedQueries in querySplitting.ts, and splitQueriesByStreamShard here) — already maps targets through applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). With the new .map(...) added here in runShardSplitQuery and the one added in runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts), every sub-query in the time-splitting path is interpolated twice, and every sub-query in the shard-splitting path three times (runShardSplitQuery → runSplitQuery → runQuery), because sub-requests keep the original request.scopedVars and request.filters. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters from request.filters are injected into the stream selector on every pass, so the LogQL selectors sent to Loki contain each ad hoc matcher two or three times (previously they were injected exactly once, in runQuery); (2) any variable value that itself contains template syntax (a constant/text variable holding a literal containing another variable's name, or a $-prefixed token) is interpolated again by the later passes, silently altering the query Loki executes. The updated shard-splitting test that expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single-target request (1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 1 per shard group in runSplitQuery, with runQuery mocked) shows the redundancy is being baked into the tests rather than eliminated. One of the interpolation layers should be removed (or the later passes skipped for already-interpolated targets).

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-act race between CountDevices and the insert allows exceeding the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first calling CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT/upsert. The count and the insert are separate, non-transactional queries. Two concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the anon_device table ends up with more devices than the configured limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (e.g., a public dashboard link being opened by many clients at once, or multiple Grafana HA replicas), the limit is only a soft cap. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a single statement with a subquery guard, a transaction with appropriate isolation, or an INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same check-then-act race: concurrent requests pass the device count check and insert beyond the limit. Both suggest a transaction or an atomic fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed on retry because the local cache is populated before the store write succeeds

In tagDeviceUI, the device cache key is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) at line 87) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the first request from a new device is correctly rejected in the anonymous auth client (client.go returns the error). However, the cache entry remains for ~29 minutes (localcache.New(29*time.Minute, ...)). Any subsequent request from the same device hits the cache at line 83, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the store, and the anonymous authentication succeeds. The consequence is that the new configurable device limit is effectively unenforced: a blocked device only sees one failed request and then gets full anonymous access by simply retrying (e.g., refreshing the browser), with the block re-asserting only once per 29-minute cache-expiry window. The cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (or the key must be removed when it returns an error).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: tagDeviceUI sets the cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs, so when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned the cache entry stays, and the device limit is bypassed for 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved from background goroutine into the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and a recover() guard, so anonymous authentication never blocked on the database write and a panic in tagging could not affect the request. This PR calls TagDevice synchronously in Authenticate for all deployments, including the default case where device_limit is unset (0) and the enforcement is not needed. On every local-cache miss (roughly once per 29 minutes per device) each anonymous request now waits for the COUNT + upsert round trips before an identity is returned, and a panic in the tagging path now propagates into request handling. Consider keeping the asynchronous path when the limit is disabled, or restoring the timeout/recover protection.

No test for the allowed path (existing device updated when limit is reached) or for repeated rejection

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a brand-new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is hit. Two important behaviors are untested: (1) that a device already present in anon_device is still successfully updated (updateDevice returns nil) when count >= deviceLimit — this is the intended happy path that keeps existing devices working, and a regression there would lock out legitimate users; (2) that a rejected device keeps being rejected on subsequent TagDevice/CreateOrUpdateDevice attempts — a test through AnonDeviceService.TagDevice would have caught the local-cache bypass where the second request from a blocked device succeeds.

New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini

The PR introduces cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from key 'device_limit' in the [auth.anonymous] section, but it does not add the option to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where the other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented with comments. As shipped, the setting is undiscoverable for administrators and its semantics (0 = unlimited, limit counted over devices active in the last 30 days) are undocumented.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation LRU cache key ignores the site-specific fallback locale

The cache key for memoized translations is built only from the key, the current locale and the backend object id (`k = "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`). With this PR, the resolved value of a translation now also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (via `FallbackLocaleList`), and that setting is per-site on multisite installs and can be changed at runtime — but it is not part of the cache key, and the cache itself (`@cache` on the I18n singleton) is process-global. Consequences: (1) on a multisite cluster sharing one process, a key missing in locale X is resolved through whichever site's default locale populated the cache first — e.g. a user on a site whose default is German can be served the French fallback string cached for another site, until the 300-entry LRU happens to evict it; (2) on a single site, after an admin changes `default_locale`, fallback strings in the old language keep being served from the cache until eviction. Previously (`config.i18n.fallbacks = true`) the fallback target was the global `I18n.default_locale`, so cached entries were consistent. Include `SiteSetting.default_locale` (or the resolved fallback chain) in the cache key, or clear `I18n`'s cache when the setting changes.

Fallback locale files are only loaded for controller requests, so fallbacks silently fail in jobs/mailers/rake

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked from the `set_locale` before_filter, i.e. only for HTTP requests through ApplicationController. The translate accelerator's `translate` only ever loads yml files for `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale)`); it never loads the fallback locales itself. Any server-side code that translates outside a web request — Sidekiq jobs, ActionMailer views, rake tasks, console — with `I18n.locale` set to a non-English locale will walk the fallback chain (locale → site default → :en), find that no translations were ever loaded for the fallback locales, and render "translation missing: xx.yyy" instead of the site-default/English string. So the feature this PR adds silently does not work in exactly the server-side contexts that don't pass through a controller. Load the fallback locales inside the accelerator instead (e.g. have `I18n.ensure_loaded!`/`translate` load every locale in `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`), or route jobs/mailers through the same ensure_loaded! step.

FallbackLocaleList#[] does a SiteSetting read and several array allocations on every interpolated translation

The i18n fallbacks backend calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every backend lookup, and `FallbackLocaleList#[]` performs a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read plus `[locale, ...].uniq.compact` (multiple array allocations) each time. The translate accelerator only memoizes argument-free lookups — every `I18n.t` call with interpolation options (the common case in this codebase, e.g. anything with `count:` or a username) bypasses the LRU cache and pays this cost per call, in a code path that exists specifically to make translation fast. Consider memoizing the computed list keyed by (locale, default_locale) and invalidating when the setting changes.

No tests for the new fallback semantics, which now apply to all environments

This PR rewrites how fallbacks are computed (new `FallbackLocaleList`, new `I18n.ensure_loaded!`, per-request `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`) and, as a side effect, enables fallbacks in every environment — previously they were only turned on via `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in the production-like configs, so in development/test a key present in English but missing in the active locale now silently renders the English text instead of a "translation missing" message. No specs cover any of this. At minimum, add coverage that `I18n.fallbacks[:xx]` returns `[xx, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq`, that a key missing in the active locale resolves through the site default and then English, and that the fallback locale files are actually loaded (the `ensure_loaded!` path).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

If `host` is nil (e.g. an API call to POST /admin/embeddable_hosts without a host value), this raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a validation error. update/destroy 500 on unknown id instead of 404

In update and destroy, the result of EmbeddableHost.where(...).first is never checked, so a missing record is nil and calling methods on it raises NoMethodError. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hosts saved with a port can never match; input host not downcased for comparison

Fabricator file contents were swapped

The INSERT interpolates the setting value directly: `VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. A value containing a single quote (legacy/malformed data in the old free-text setting) will produce invalid SQL and abort the migration. Use `ActiveRecord::Base.sanitize`/`quote` or a parameterized insert.

The candidate stresses broken SQL from single quotes rather than security, but the underlying issue is the same. The file path differs (golden names the controller, the candidate implies a migration), yet it is clearly the same INSERT code.

embed_category is deleted even when no host rows were created

If a site used feed polling with `embed_category` set but had no `embeddable_hosts` configured (feed-only embedding, which previously worked because `TopicEmbed.import` used the global `SiteSetting.embed_category`), this migration creates zero `embeddable_hosts` rows and still deletes the `embed_category` setting. The previously configured category assignment is lost with no replacement.

Migration is not reversible despite using `change`

The migration uses `def change` but contains raw `execute` statements (data copy and `DELETE FROM site_settings`). Rolling back will raise ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration, and even a manual reverse can't restore the deleted `embeddable_hosts`/`embed_category` setting rows. This should be split into `up`/`down` with an explicit, safe down (or acknowledge irreversibility).

No foreign key or cleanup for category_id

`category_id` is `null: false` but has no foreign key, and the `EmbeddableHost` model has no `belongs_to` presence validation or dependent handling. Deleting a category leaves dangling `embeddable_hosts.category_id` values; `TopicEmbed.import` will then create topics pointing at a nonexistent category (PostCreator is given the stale id, and `ensure_topic_has_a_category` won't fix it since the id isn't nil), and the admin UI renders a missing category badge. show always renders JSON, so direct navigation/refresh to /admin/customize/embedding breaks

`show` unconditionally calls `render_serialized(...)`, which renders JSON for every format. The sibling customize pages (permalinks, colors, emojis, site texts) respond with an HTML page that boots the Ember admin app for non-XHR requests; this controller (and its missing view template) does not. Opening or refreshing `https://site/admin/customize/embedding` directly in a browser returns a raw JSON payload instead of the admin UI. Add `respond_to`/`format.html` handling plus the blank HTML view like the other admin customize controllers.

No uniqueness constraint on host

Neither the model nor the migration enforces uniqueness of `host`. The admin UI lets the same host be added multiple times with different categories, and `record_for_host` uses `.first`, so which category an embedded topic lands in becomes nondeterministic. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host` and a unique index (the migration's data copy should also dedupe).

The regex requires `\.[a-z]{2,5}` for the final label, so valid domains like `example.technology`, `example.international` or `example.museum` fail validation and can't be added as embedding hosts. The old free-text setting imposed no such restriction, so this is a new, undocumented limitation.

Test 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' no longer tests what it claims

`Topic#expandable_first_post?` was changed to `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?` and no longer consults embeddable hosts at all. The example should be renamed/rewritten to reflect the new contract (or removed).

The specs for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` (and `Admin::EmbeddingController`) only assert the class inherits from `Admin::AdminController`. All the actual behavior added in this PR — creating/updating a host, the fallback to `uncategorized_category_id` when category is blank, validation errors, unknown-id handling, destroy, and the embedding show payload — is completely untested, which is how the nil-record and nil-param crashes slip through.

UsersController#create (app/controllers/users_controller.rb) calls user.valid? on line 168 and then user.save on line 172, both of which run the full validation suite, so a single signup attempt with a blocked email increments match_count by 2 and updates last_match_at twice. The match_count/last_match_at statistics (whose purpose is explicitly described in the specs) will therefore be wrong for the primary flow they were built for. The stats update should be separated from validation (e.g. done once in the controller when a block actually rejects the signup) or made idempotent per request. should_block? loads the record, does record.match_count += 1, then record.save. Two concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email both read the same match_count and one increment is lost. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is dead code — missing '?' so AMS never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers decides whether to serialize an attribute by calling `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark), as used everywhere else in this file (`include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc.). The added method is named `include_website_name` without the `?`, so it is never invoked and `website_name` is always included in the payload — serialized as explicit null for users who have no website — instead of being omitted when `website` is blank. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (or, better, add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` as noted in the other finding, which also defines the include predicate).

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the TL0/anonymous restriction that hides website

The serializer deliberately hides `website` (along with bio, location, etc.) for trust-level-0 users viewed by anonymous visitors via the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism (`include_website?` returns false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`). The new `website_name` attribute is not in the `untrusted_attributes` list, and its value is derived directly from `object.user_profile.website`, so anonymous visitors now receive `website_name` (the website's host, plus full path when it matches the instance domain) in the JSON for TL0 users even though `website` itself is withheld. This defeats the anti-spam purpose of restricting those fields. The existing spec 'doesn't serialize untrusted attributes' will not catch this because `website_name` isn't in its attribute list either. Fix by adding `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or checking `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` in its include guard) and extend the spec to cover it.

Websites Ruby's URI parser rejects (e.g. IDN/Unicode domains) disappear from the profile entirely

`URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` returns nil for any stored website that Ruby's ASCII-only URI parser cannot handle, such as non-ASCII/IDN domains. `website_name` then returns nil, and since the template renders the globe icon and link only inside `{{#if model.website_name}}`, the user's website stops being displayed on their profile at all. The previous client-side code (`website.split("/")[2]`) still displayed the domain for such URLs, so this is a regression for affected users. Consider falling back to the raw `website` string when URI parsing fails instead of returning nil.

No test for the sibling-subdomain branch of website_name

The most complex branch of `website_name` — the `elsif` that compares parent domains when website and instance hosts have equal label depth greater than 2 (e.g. show the full path for `www.example.com` on a `forum.example.com` instance, but only the host for `www.other.com`) — has no test coverage. The three added examples only exercise the equal-host case and the website-domain-is-parent case, so a regression in the parent-domain comparison would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into href attribute of posts rendered as raw HTML TopicEmbed.import appends an 'Imported from' footer built as "#{url}" with the URL inserted unescaped. The only validation is that the URL starts with http(s)://; a single quote is a valid URI character, so a feed item link or an embed URL like http://host/page'onmouseover='alert(1) breaks out of the href attribute and injects arbitrary attributes/markup into the post body. Because these posts are created with cook_method raw_html, Post#cook returns the raw string with no sanitization, and the embed view renders it via `raw post.cooked` (and the main site renders cooked verbatim), this becomes stored XSS on the forum origin for everyone who views the imported topic or embed. Escape the URL (e.g. ERB::Util.html_escape) before interpolating it into the attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment raises two issues: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and XSS from unescaped url interpolation. The candidate covers the XSS part in detail, describing the same unescaped URL in the generated HTML. It does not mention the nil case, but the XSS issue is a core part of the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed items without content crash the polling job permanently

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` raises NoMethodError when an item has no content element. With simple-rss, RSS 2.0 items only expose #content when the feed includes <content:encoded>; a large number of feeds carry only <description>, and Atom entries may omit content too. One such item raises out of the each loop, aborting the whole poll (the job has retry: false), and since items are processed in feed order the same item crashes the job again on every hourly run, so no later items are ever imported. Fall back to i.description / to_s and wrap per-item processing so one bad item cannot kill the entire feed poll.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: i.content.scrub fails when content is nil, which is common in RSS feeds that only carry description. Both also propose falling back to description.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer injected into a JavaScript string with only HTML escaping

The embed layout interpolates request.referer directly into a single-quoted JS string: parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>'). ERB output is HTML-escaped, which is the wrong escaping context for a JavaScript string — and in the Rails 3 boot mode this repo still supports, ERB's html_escape does not escape single quotes at all. A request to /embed/best with a Referer such as http://<embeddable-host>/';alert(1);// passes the ensure_embeddable host check (a single quote and semicolons are legal characters in a URI path) and breaks out of the JS string, executing arbitrary script inside the iframe on the forum's own origin. Use request.referer.to_json (or escape_javascript) when building the targetOrigin string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without JS-context escaping, which allows XSS. The candidate gives more detail, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method renders remotely fetched content with zero sanitization

Post#cook now returns `raw` unchanged when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing PrettyText's sanitizer entirely. The content stored in these posts comes from remote sources: feed items via PollFeed (no filtering at all) and arbitrary pages on the embeddable host via TopicRetriever/import_remote (ruby-readability whitelists tags/attributes but still passes through href/src values such as javascript: URLs). Any script, event handler, or javascript: link in the source HTML is rendered verbatim on topic pages, in the embed iframe on the forum origin, in email digests, etc. Additionally, PostCreator now honors opts[:cook_method] for every caller (lib/post_creator.rb setup_post) — if request parameters ever flow into PostCreator opts, any user could create unsanitized raw-HTML posts, so this must be guarded against.

TopicEmbed row is created even when PostCreator rolled the post back, leaving a dangling reference

import only checks `if post.present?` before calling TopicEmbed.create!, but PostCreator#create returns the unsaved post object (with errors) when creation fails — for example when rollback_if_host_spam_detected fires, which happens for a trust-level-0 embed user importing an article that links several times to the same host (newuser_spam_host_threshold). In that case the inner Post transaction rolls back the topic and post inserts, but TopicEmbed.create! still commits a row whose topic_id/post_id point at records that no longer exist. Every subsequent /embed/best request for that URL then finds the dead topic_id and TopicView raises not-found/invalid-access, so the embed for that URL is permanently broken and the import is never retried. Check post.persisted? / post.errors.empty? instead of post.present?.

absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs Both the and rewriting treat any value starting with '/' as root-relative and rewrite it to prefix + path. Protocol-relative URLs such as //cdn.example.com/image.png (common in feeds and CMS output) also start with '/', so they are rewritten to http://host/cdn.example.com/image.png, breaking the link or image. Values starting with '//' should be left alone.

Unauthenticated endpoint enqueues unbounded outbound-fetch jobs

Any GET to /embed/best whose Referer host matches embeddable_host (a header trivially forged by non-browser clients) and that carries a previously unseen embed_url enqueues a RetrieveTopic job, which performs an outbound HTTP fetch of that URL. The only throttle is a 60-second redis key per URL inside the job, so an attacker can enqueue unlimited jobs simply by varying the URL — exhausting sidekiq workers and directing a flood of fetches at the configured embeddable host. There should be a global or per-IP rate limit before enqueuing retrieval work.

Every new embed URL runs a full synchronous feed poll

When feed_polling_enabled? is on, perform_retrieve executes Jobs::PollFeed inline for each retrieval before falling back to direct HTTP fetch. The retrieval throttle is keyed per embed URL, so N distinct new embed URLs cause N full feed downloads/parses (and a re-import/revision pass over every feed item) inside RetrieveTopic jobs. The unused feed_key method on PollFeed suggests a per-feed throttle was intended but never wired up.

Missing Referer hard-fails embedding for legitimate visitors

ensure_embeddable raises Discourse::InvalidAccess when request.referer is blank. Visitors using referer-stripping privacy extensions, behind referer-removing proxies, or on an HTTPS page embedding an HTTP forum (browsers omit Referer on the HTTPS→HTTP downgrade) will get an error instead of the comment embed. The check only needs to reject referers from foreign hosts; a blank referer could be treated as allowed so these users still see comments.

Disqus import no longer preserves the thread's original creation date

Before this change the topic-opening post was created with created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]); the new code path calls TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title]), which provides no way to pass created_at, so every imported thread's opening post is timestamped at import time. Imported forums lose their original chronology (topic ordering, 'x days ago' dates, digest ordering). Add a created_at option to import/import_remote and pass the thread date through.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
self.downsize is defined twice; the 4-argument version is dead and old callers silently misbehave

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: lines 145-147 (`from, to, max_width, max_height, opts`) and lines 149-151 (`from, to, dimensions, opts`). Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the first method is dead code. Worse, any existing or plugin caller still using the old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, width, height)` gets no arity error: the width is used verbatim as the ImageMagick geometry string (e.g. `-resize 1920\>` with no height) and the height (an Integer) is used as `opts`, so `!!opts[:allow_animation]` in `optimize` raises TypeError (Integer#[] with a Symbol), which is not rescued because the rescue lives in `convert_with`. Remove the leftover 4-argument definition (or make it delegate to the new one correctly).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The downsize method is defined twice, and the later dimensions-string version overrides the width/height version. As a result, callers that pass separate width and height arguments break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client upload size check hardcodes 10MB for all types, ignoring the per-type site settings

`validateUploadedFile` now caps every upload at `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. The server-side downsize added in this PR only applies to images; attachments are still validated against `max_attachment_size_kb`, so sites with a lower attachment limit now accept files client-side that the server then rejects (bad UX, wasted upload), and sites with a higher attachment limit (or `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB) now have legitimate uploads blocked client-side — a regression. The 413 error handler at line 246 likewise always reports a 10MB limit in the `file_too_large` message regardless of the actual configured limit. Keep the per-type setting for attachments and only raise the effective cap for images that the server can downsize.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same problem as the golden comment: the hardcoded 10MB limit ignores the per-type site settings, so client and server limits can diverge. It also notes that the 413 handler is affected in the same way.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Large animated GIFs are silently flattened to their first frame

The downsize call passes `tempfile.path` as `from`, and `OptimizedImage.optimize` only selects the animated (gifsicle) code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. Upload tempfiles created by Rack (and the API download tempfile) do not carry the original file extension, so for normal composer uploads this check is always false and a large animated GIF is processed by `convert from[0] ...`, whose `[0]` selects only the first frame and writes a static image back over the user's original file — the animation is silently destroyed even when `allow_animation` is enabled. Additionally, even when the animated branch is reached, it is handed the geometry string "80%", but gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects an explicit WxH geometry and does not accept percentages, so it would fail on every one of the 5 attempts (the loop also ignores `downsize`'s false return and just retries the identical command). Base the animation check on the original filename or content type rather than the tempfile path, and use gifsicle-compatible geometry.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main point is different: the tempfile has no extension, so animated GIFs get flattened to one frame. It also states the golden issue directly: gifsicle's --resize-fit does not accept the "80%" geometry, so downsizing fails on the animated path. Because that point is explicitly included, the candidate matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsanitized `type` param flows into a shell command via the tempfile path (command injection)

`type` comes directly from `params` and is embedded into the download tempfile name ("discourse-upload-#{type}") at line 55. This PR then passes `tempfile.path` to `OptimizedImage.downsize` (line 67), and `OptimizedImage.convert_with` executes the instructions with backticks (`` `#{instructions.join(" ")}` `` in optimized_image.rb) with no shell escaping. A caller who can use the API URL-upload branch (`is_api?` + `url` present, no file) can put shell metacharacters such as `$(...)` or backticks into `type`; hosting an image larger than `max_image_size_kb` at that URL makes the new downsize branch execute, running the injected command as the app server user. Previously this tempfile path never reached a shell, so this exposure is introduced by this PR. Validate `type` against a whitelist before using it in a filename, and/or stop interpolating paths into a shell string (use an argv-array form of exec instead of backticks).

API URL-download cap hardcoded to 10MB and nil tempfile still dereferenced

For API uploads by URL the download limit was changed from the configured `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a fixed `10.megabytes`. This branch also serves non-image uploads, so attachments larger than 10MB can no longer be pulled via the API even when `max_attachment_size_kb` permits them. When the cap is exceeded the `rescue nil` leaves `tempfile` as nil, and line 72 then calls `tempfile.size`, raising NoMethodError instead of returning a clean error to the API client. Use the per-type size setting and handle the nil tempfile case explicitly.

No tests for the new auto-downsize behavior

The new downsize loop in `create_upload` (lines 64-70) — a retry loop that shells out to ImageMagick/gifsicle and mutates the uploaded file before `Upload.create_for` — ships without any spec coverage. There are no tests verifying that an over-limit image is downsized and accepted, that an image still over the limit after 5 attempts returns a clean validation error, or that animated GIFs keep their animation (they currently do not). Add controller/model specs covering these cases.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when no TopicUser row exists and bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (the user may have no row for that topic — e.g., it was never created or was removed), and the very next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`, producing a NoMethodError and a 500 instead of unsubscribing. Separately, assigning `notification_level` directly and calling `save!` skips what `TopicUser.change` does: it does not set `notifications_reason_id`/`notifications_changed_at` and does not publish the MessageBus `notification_level_change` event. Because `notifications_reason_id` remains NULL, the auto-track SQL in `TopicUser.update_last_read` (`when tu.notifications_reason_id is null and total_msecs_viewed > threshold then :tracking`) will silently flip the user back to tracking the next time they read posts in that topic, undoing their explicit unsubscribe, and other open browser tabs will show stale notification state. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`, which upserts safely (no nil crash), records the reason, and broadcasts the change.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says find_by can return nil and that dereferencing tu.notification_level then crashes. That is the same nil pointer issue the golden comment describes. The extra bookkeeping concerns don't change the match.

false_positives.candidate: Topic unsubscribe mutates user state via an unprotected GET request The new `topics#unsubscribe` action is routed as `GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` and `GET /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe`, and it changes the current user's TopicUser notification level (demoting tracking/watching to regular, or muting) as a side effect of a plain GET. Rails does not verify CSRF tokens on GET requests, and the controller also skips `check_xhr` for this action, so any content that causes a logged-in user's browser to request that URL will silently change their subscription state. Concretely: an attacker can embed `` in a post, PM, or external page and every logged-in viewer gets muted/unsubscribed from topic 123. Additionally, corporate email gateways and security link-scanners that fetch URLs found in incoming mail will trigger the unsubscribe without the user ever clicking. The GET should render a confirmation page only, with the actual change performed via a POST/PUT (protected by the CSRF token) or via a signed one-click-unsubscribe token.

Unsubscribe toggle is not idempotent — reloading the page changes state again

In `topics#unsubscribe`, the new level is computed by toggling off the current level: if `tu.notification_level > regular` it is set to `regular`, otherwise it is set to `muted`. Because the mutation runs on every GET of the unsubscribe URL, repeating the request keeps changing the user's state: a watching user is demoted to regular on first load and then fully muted if they simply refresh the confirmation page (or hit back/forward, or a prefetcher re-fetches the link). Meanwhile the page text says "You will stop receiving notifications for …", which no longer matches the state the user actually ends up in after a reload. The action should set a deterministic target level (e.g., always mute, or always regular) or defer the change to an explicit form submission, so repeated visits are harmless.

Client-side navigation to /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe claims the user was unsubscribed without unsubscribing them

The actual unsubscribe only happens server-side in `topics#unsubscribe` during a full page load. The new Ember route's model hook merely loads the topic (`PostStream.loadTopicView`) and never calls any unsubscribe endpoint, yet its template states "You will stop receiving notifications for <topic>". Discourse intercepts clicks on same-origin links (for example an unsubscribe URL posted inside a topic or PM) and transitions client-side without a server round-trip, so a user arriving that way sees a message asserting they were unsubscribed when nothing changed — the opposite result from opening the same URL in a new tab, which does unsubscribe them. The route should either perform the change (e.g., via the notifications endpoint) or the copy should not claim notifications have stopped.

No request specs for the new state-changing topics#unsubscribe endpoint

This PR adds a new public, state-changing controller action plus routes, but the only spec touched is `spec/components/email/message_builder_spec.rb` (passing an extra `unsubscribe_url` option). There is no controller/request coverage for: unsubscribing from each starting level (watching/tracking/regular/muted), behavior when no TopicUser row exists, the 301 slug redirect, or the login requirement. Given the non-idempotent toggle logic and the nil-handling risk in this action, the endpoint needs request specs before merge.

unsubscribe_link now requires an %{unsubscribe_url} interpolation argument, breaking other add_unsubscribe_link callers

The default `unsubscribe_link` text now embeds `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` render it via `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` for every email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. All core notification mailers were updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`, but any other existing or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` (e.g., plugin mailers) will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and fail to send, where previously it worked. Consider putting the per-topic sentence in a separate optional translation key or defaulting `unsubscribe_url` (e.g., to the user preferences URL) inside MessageBuilder.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only; script fails on GNU/Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` uses BSD/macOS sed syntax. With GNU sed (Linux), `-i` does not take a separate empty suffix argument, so the command misparses the arguments and fails ('can't read s|...|'), meaning GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines. Use a portable approach (write to a temp file and mv, or detect the sed flavor).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the `sed -i ''` syntax only works with BSD/macOS sed and fails on GNU/Linux.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handler throws plain Error, producing a 500 instead of a 404/403

When the credential doesn't exist or belongs to another user, deleteCacheHandler throws a generic `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a non-TRPCError is converted to an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) and is typically reported to error monitoring as a server bug, rather than a client-facing NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" })` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: a generic Error is thrown on an auth/access failure, which tRPC turns into a 500. Both say to throw a TRPCError instead. The candidate suggests the NOT_FOUND code rather than FORBIDDEN, but it names 403 as an option too, so the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting

The 'Last updated' timestamp is rendered with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, forcing US date/time formatting on all users regardless of their configured locale, in a product that is otherwise fully localized (the surrounding labels go through t()). Use the user's locale (e.g. navigator.language or dayjs with the user's locale) so the timestamp respects localization.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the date is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of the user's locale. The candidate suggests a slightly different fix (navigator.language or dayjs rather than useLocale), but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in the UI

In CredentialActionsDropdown, the deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component (lines 61-64), it never invalidates trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. The cacheUpdatedAt value driving the 'Cache Status / Last updated' display comes from that query, so after a user deletes the cache the dropdown continues to show the old timestamp and the 'Delete cached data' option until something else happens to refetch — making it look as if the deletion failed. Add an invalidation of viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (e.g. in onSettled) for the deleteCache mutation, as was done for disconnect.

Migration backfills updatedAt with NOW() for all existing rows and forces a full table rewrite

ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW() has two problems. (1) Because NOW() is not a constant default, PostgreSQL must rewrite the entire CalendarCache table to add the column, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration — on a large/busy cache table this can block writes during deployment. (2) Every pre-existing row gets updatedAt = migration time, so the new UI will display 'Last updated: <deploy time>' for all existing caches, which is misleading until each row is next written. Safer approach: add the column nullable (metadata-only operation), backfill in batches or leave legacy rows null, and hide the timestamp in the UI when it is null.

Handler bypasses the calendar-cache feature flag by instantiating the concrete repository

connectedCalendarsHandler constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of using the feature-flag-aware factory (CalendarCache.init(...)), which returns CalendarCacheRepositoryMock when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. This PR even adds getCacheStatusByCredentialIds to the mock (returning []), but that path can never be reached from this handler. Consequence: users/teams without the calendar-cache feature still get cache status and delete actions surfaced (from any stale rows), and every connectedCalendars request pays the extra groupBy query even when the feature is turned off.

Cache status query does not exclude expired cache rows

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups over all CalendarCache rows for the given credentials without filtering on expiresAt, while the read path (getCachedAvailability) only serves rows with expiresAt >= now(). The UI can therefore show 'Cache Status: Last updated X' and offer 'Delete cached data' for a cache that has already expired and is never served; after deletion nothing visibly changes for the user. Apply the same expiresAt filter (or surface the expiry state in the UI) so status matches what is actually usable.

Dead write: SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is bumped on every webhook cache refresh but never read

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache — which runs on every Google webhook-driven cache refresh — now executes SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}), an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row for the credential, solely to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. Per the PR's own notes this value is not displayed anywhere (the frontend uses cacheUpdatedAt from CalendarCache), and nothing else in the diff reads it; the change also forced extra selected fields in UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession and the UserWithCalendars type to carry an unused value. This is a pure extra write on a hot webhook path and should be removed or deferred until a consumer exists.

ENV_FILE="../.env" is resolved relative to the caller's CWD, not the script location

ENV_FILE is a relative path, so its target depends on where the script is invoked from. Running it from the repo root (./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh) writes GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL to a .env file in the repository's parent directory (creating a stray file via the touch fallback) and never updates the project's actual .env. Resolve the env file path from the script's own directory (e.g. using BASH_SOURCE) so it works regardless of the invocation directory.

No tests for the new cache-status repository method or the deleteCache authorization

The PR adds user-facing destructive behavior with no test coverage: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds (grouping/max(updatedAt) semantics, empty credentialIds input, expired rows) and deleteCacheHandler's authorization rule (a user must not be able to delete another user's calendar cache by supplying an arbitrary credentialId). Only the mock repository was updated; the real implementation and the new tRPC handler have no tests, and the PR description itself notes end-to-end testing was not performed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours guard computes the slot end from the slot start time

In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is an exact copy of the `start` computation — it never adds eventLength, so the upper-bound comparison `end > workingHour.endTime` only checks the slot's start. When EventManager creates the event for a non-organizer host's CalDAV credential (collective events), that host's account does not contain the main host's calendar URL, so the filtered list is empty, `Promise.all([])` resolves to `[]`, `responses.some(r => !r.ok)` is false, and the method returns a successful result with a uid — but no event was created anywhere. This is a silent data-integrity failure: the booking reference is stored, but the team member's calendar has no event. It should match the destination calendar for the credential in use, like Google's credentialId lookup.

Team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer and event type have none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists, and the collective-team calendars are added via `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining means that when the base value is `null`, the push is silently skipped: for a collective event where the organizer has no connected destination calendar but team members do, none of the team members' calendars receive events (and the booking's destinationCalendar is not connected either). The array should be initialized to `[]` (or the team calendars assigned directly) so collective hosts still get their events.

Dynamic user query no longer selects organization

The `loadUsers` refactor rewrote the dynamic-group user lookup and dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select (it was explicitly selected before, together with `metadata`). Any downstream code for dynamic collective bookings that reads `user.organization.slug` (e.g. org-subdomain/booker-url handling) will now get `undefined` and potentially throw. This removal is unrelated to the destination-calendar change and looks accidental; it should be restored.

Recurring-event deletion block now runs once per calendar reference

The recurring-cancellation branch (mapping over all of the organizer's calendar credentials × all updated recurring bookings and deleting each) lives inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the collective multi-host case this PR introduces, typically one per host), the entire recurring deletion pass executes once per reference, issuing duplicate `deleteEvent` calls for the same events. Google tolerates this via 404/410 handling, but other providers may log errors and it doubles the external API traffic. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop. (Separately, that branch still only deletes the first calendar reference per updated booking, so team-member calendar events for recurring collective bookings remain stale.)

Hangout-link patch call uses possibly-undefined calendarId

In `createEvent`, the insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` (that writes the description with the hangout link) passes the raw `selectedCalendar`, which is `undefined` whenever no destination calendar matches the credentialId. The google client will throw a missing-parameter error for that patch, so the hangout link is never written into the event description in that case. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always defined (defaulted to "primary").

Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging bookings on reschedule

When `newBookingId` is set (reschedule/merge path), the code deletes the old booking's calendar event via `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`. Bookings can now have multiple calendar references (one per collective host), so only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep a stale event at the old time. This should iterate over all calendar references of the old booking.

Webhook payload sends destinationCalendar as null in some flows and [] in others

The updated e2e expectations now encode that BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED payloads contain `destinationCalendar: null` while BOOKING_REJECTED contains `destinationCalendar: []` — because handleNewBooking emits `null` when there is no destination calendar while confirm.handler emits `[]`. This is an inconsistent contract for the same field across webhook triggers, and the field's shape also changed from a single object to an array, which is a breaking change for existing webhook consumers despite the PR being labelled non-breaking. Consider normalizing (always array, or always null-when-empty) across all emitters.

No automated tests cover the new multi-destination calendar logic

The PR rewrites `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` and the create/update/delete paths of four calendar providers for the collective multi-host scenario, but the author explicitly checked "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". The only test change is a webhook payload expectation. Regressions introduced here (e.g. the Google Meet fallback TypeError, non-Google providers writing to the main host's calendar, video references losing credentialId) would be caught by even a minimal unit test around `EventManager.create` with multiple destination calendars.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
App API dispatcher still reads the appStore barrel synchronously, breaking all app OAuth callbacks and app webhooks

This PR changes every value of the default export of `@calcom/app-store` from the app's module namespace to a Promise of that namespace. The catch-all API route `apps/web/pages/api/integrations/[...args].ts`, which dispatches every app's API endpoints (`/api/integrations/{app}/add`, `/callback`, `/webhook`, etc. — e.g. the Google Calendar OAuth callback and the Stripe payment webhooks) looks the app up synchronously as `const app = appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` and then checks `"api" in app` before calling `app.api[endpoint](req, res)`. It is not among the updated files, so after this change `app` is a Promise, the `in` check is false, and the route falls through to its error/404 path for every app. Consequence: connecting/disconnecting any integration and all payment webhooks stop working. The lookup must become `const app = await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]`. It is also worth grepping the whole repo for any other remaining `appStore[...]` / `getCalendar(` consumers, since the barrel's contract changed from synchronous module to Promise and only the call sites in this PR were migrated.

The dynamic imports still execute eagerly — importing the barrel immediately loads all 28 app chunks

Each registry entry is written as `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`, so every `import()` expression is invoked at the moment `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. Only the *awaiting* became lazy, not the *loading*: the first import of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers fetching and evaluating all 28 app modules, so the startup/module-load cost this PR is presumably trying to reduce is essentially unchanged (only code-splitting/parallel async evaluation is gained). If the intent is to load an app only when it is actually used, the values need to be thunks (`() => import("./applecalendar")`) or a lazy getter/Proxy, with call sites adjusted accordingly. A side effect of creating all 28 promises up front is that a chunk-load failure in an app that is never used still produces an unhandled promise rejection (most entries are never awaited), which crashes Node under the default unhandled-rejections behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
